intermediate representations
an IR makes particular facts easy to express. an AST preserves source structure, a control-flow graph exposes possible execution paths, and machine IR records target constraints. a compiler moves between them as the questions it needs to answer change.
abstract syntax tree
an AST represents expressions, statements, and declarations as nodes. a typed AST associates those nodes with information from semantic analysis.
a visitor traverses the nodes, an interpreter evaluates them, and a transformer constructs a revised tree. immutable nodes allow sharing without concurrent mutation; mutable trees support in-place changes with corresponding ownership requirements.
the tree is useful for source-level diagnostics and transformations. control flow is implicit in constructs such as loops and conditionals, so analyses that follow execution paths usually use a CFG instead.
control flow graph
a control-flow graph (CFG) connects basic blocks. control enters a block at its first instruction and follows its instructions to a terminator. the terminator determines its successors.
in a function-level CFG, an ordinary returning call can remain inside a block. branches and exceptional control transfers require edges; interprocedural graphs can additionally represent calls and returns across functions.
block A dominates a reachable block B when every path from the entry to B passes through A. this tells an optimizer where a computed value is guaranteed to exist. dominance frontiers identify joins where that guarantee stops holding.
static single assignment form
in static single assignment (SSA) form, each value name has one defining instruction in the program text. a loop can execute that instruction many times. each use refers to its definition, which makes value dependencies explicit.
a \phi node selects an incoming value according to the predecessor edge taken. in this pseudocode, the result at the join depends on which branch ran:

desugar a language construct into simpler constructs;
turn structured control flow into branches;
represent addressable storage with memory operations;
place arguments according to a calling convention;
select target-specific operations.

the details matter: lowering a for loop must preserve how continue reaches its update step. see XLA for tensor computations lowered through HLO and backend representations.
dataflow analysis
dataflow analysis approximates what may or must be true at each point in a program. each block transforms a set of facts; joins combine the facts from different paths. the examples below assume local scalar variables and an intraprocedural CFG. memory aliases and calls require additional effects information.
lattice theory
dataflow facts can form a lattice: a partial order with a meet \wedge and a join \vee. the order expresses the analysis’s information convention.
for a constant-propagation domain, use \bot for no feasible execution, one element for each constant, and \top for a value that may vary. distinct constants are incomparable. joining two distinct constants produces \top.
a transfer function is monotone when
a \sqsubseteq b \implies f(a) \sqsubseteq f(b).
monotonicity alone does not guarantee termination. iteration from the appropriate initial element terminates on a finite-height lattice because facts can change strictly in the chosen direction only finitely often. infinite-height domains may need widening to force convergence. soundness separately requires that transfer functions and joins conservatively cover program behavior. Clang’s dataflow introduction.
a worklist revisits blocks whose inputs may have changed. when no equation needs updating, the computed facts form a fixed point.
reaching definitions
which assignments may supply a value at a later point? a definition of x reaches p if some CFG path from the definition to p contains no intervening assignment to x.
dataflow equations:
\begin{aligned}
\text{IN}[B] &= \bigcup_{P \in \text{pred}(B)} \text{OUT}[P] \\
\text{OUT}[B] &= \text{GEN}[B] \cup (\text{IN}[B] \setminus \text{KILL}[B])
\end{aligned}
\text{GEN}[B] contains definitions in B that survive to its exit. \text{KILL}[B] contains definitions of variables assigned in B; the union with \text{GEN}[B] adds back the surviving local definitions.

liveness analysis
a variable x is live at p if some CFG path from p uses its current value before redefining it. this is a conservative possibility; the execution need not take that path.
dataflow equations:
\begin{aligned}
\text{OUT}[B] &= \bigcup_{S \in \text{succ}(B)} \text{IN}[S] \\
\text{IN}[B] &= \text{USE}[B] \cup (\text{OUT}[B] \setminus \text{DEF}[B])
\end{aligned}
\text{USE}[B] contains variables read before their first definition in B, and \text{DEF}[B] contains variables defined there. a return operand counts as a use.
this is a backward may analysis. information about a later use propagates toward definitions that could supply it. liveness helps register allocation determine which values need storage at the same time. Cornell’s worklist derivation starts with empty sets and propagates newly discovered uses.
available expressions
an expression is available at p if every path to p contains an evaluation whose operands remain unchanged afterward. availability asks whether a prior result can safely be reused.
\begin{aligned}
\text{IN}[B] &= \bigcap_{P \in \text{pred}(B)} \text{OUT}[P] \quad \text{(must property)} \\
\text{OUT}[B] &= \text{GEN}[B] \cup (\text{IN}[B] \setminus \text{KILL}[B])
\end{aligned}
\text{GEN}[B] contains evaluated expressions that remain valid at the exit. \text{KILL}[B] contains expressions whose operands are assigned in B.

optimization applications
constant propagation on SSA follows value dependencies and merges facts at \phi nodes. sparse conditional constant propagation (SCCP) also tracks executable edges, which can make a join constant when one branch is unreachable.
dead code elimination removes computations that cannot affect required behavior. an unused SSA result is a candidate, but a call may still write memory, throw, or fail to terminate. a value absent from block-exit liveness can also have a use earlier inside that block. the instruction’s effects and the language or IR semantics determine whether deletion is legal.
common subexpression elimination reuses an equivalent available value. global value numbering groups equivalent computations; dominance and effects constrain where reuse is valid. two loads from the same address can differ if an intervening operation writes through an alias.
LLVM’s pass reference describes SCCP, dead-code elimination, and value numbering as separate analyses and transformations.

final compilation phases produce machine code.
register allocation
register allocation assigns virtual values to a limited set of physical registers. when values cannot all remain in registers, the allocator inserts spills and reloads or recomputes cheap values.
interference graph: nodes represent live ranges; an edge forbids two ranges from sharing a register. SSA \phi operands are used on their incoming edges, so operands from mutually exclusive paths should not automatically interfere at the join.
graph coloring: with k interchangeable registers, a node with fewer than k neighbors can be removed temporarily and colored after its neighbors. high-degree nodes are candidates for spilling; degree alone does not prove that a spill is necessary. real targets add register classes, fixed operands, and calling-convention constraints.
linear scan processes live intervals in start order, expires finished intervals, and chooses a range to spill when registers run out. sorting and active-set management also cost time. splitting intervals can recover precision lost when one interval covers holes in a value’s lifetime.

advanced techniques include coalescing copies and splitting live ranges. lowering \phi nodes introduces edge copies; successful coalescing lets those copies disappear. LLVM’s greedy allocator combines eviction with live-range splitting.
instruction selection
instruction selection maps IR operations to instructions supported by the target. a selector can cover an expression tree with patterns and minimize a chosen cost, such as code size.
pattern matching: BURG-style selectors use bottom-up dynamic programming over tree patterns. these illustrative integer patterns assume that the target supports the corresponding instructions:

ADD(a, CONST(c))  -> add-immediate a, c
ADD(a, b)        -> add a, b
ADD(MUL(a, b), c) -> multiply-add a, b, c

operand widths, immediate ranges, and instruction costs belong to the target description. a floating-point fused multiply-add has one rounding step, so selecting it for separate multiply and add operations requires permission under the floating-point contract.
DAG-based selection can represent shared computations without duplicating tree nodes. LLVM’s SelectionDAG pipeline also legalizes unsupported operations and types. LLVM has a GlobalISel pipeline as well; SelectionDAG is one implementation. LLVM code generator.
complexity depends on the representation and cost model. a locally cheapest pattern can increase register pressure or prevent another useful pattern. production selectors combine pattern rules with heuristics because minimum instruction count alone does not predict execution time.
instruction scheduling
scheduling orders instructions subject to dependencies and machine resources. a list scheduler selects from instructions whose dependencies have been satisfied.
dependencies include read-after-write, write-after-read, and write-after-write. register renaming can remove name-based dependencies. memory operations also need alias and ordering information before they can move past one another.
software pipelining overlaps work from different loop iterations. modulo scheduling seeks a repeating schedule with a chosen initiation interval, subject to resource and loop-carried dependence limits. prologue and epilogue code handle entering and leaving that schedule.
latency hiding places independent work between a long-latency operation and its consumer. moving a load earlier can help, though keeping its result alive longer raises register pressure. cache level, hardware, and surrounding work determine the latency worth hiding.
see XLA for scheduling tensor operations and managing their buffers.
machine learning compilers
ML compilers operate on tensor programs whose operations expose shapes, element types, and data dependencies. this gives the compiler information for choosing layouts, combining kernels, and reusing buffers.
XLA (accelerated linear algebra)
TensorFlow can send a function’s tensor computation to XLA by requesting compilation explicitly:

import tensorflow as tf
 
 
@tf.function(jit_compile=True)
def compute(x, y, z):
  return tf.reduce_sum(x + y * z)
 
 
# inspect the generated HLO and profile the actual inputs
tf.function traces a TensorFlow graph; jit_compile=True requests XLA compilation for that function. OpenXLA’s TensorFlow tutorial shows this boundary and how to inspect compiler output. see XLA for fusion algorithms.
fusion can avoid materializing intermediate tensors and reduce kernel launches. the reduction’s shape, target, and compiler decisions determine the generated kernels. a fixed launch count or bandwidth ratio cannot be inferred from the three source operations. XLA’s GPU architecture describes fusion, layouts, and buffer assignment.
compute graphs as ir
this graph represents the captured computation \sum_i (x_i + y_i z_i) for equally shaped vectors:

graph LR
    A[Input x] --> E[Add]
    B[Input y] --> D
    D --> E[Add]
    C[Input z] --> D[Multiply]
    E --> F[ReduceSum]
    F --> G[Output]

the graph exposes dependencies within the captured region. an optimizer can fold constants, reuse equivalent expressions, or combine producer and consumer operations. each rewrite must respect element types, shapes, side effects, and floating-point rules. reordering a reduction can change its rounding.
graph capture does not imply that the entire application was captured or that tracing happens only once. JAX caches compiled specializations and can retrace for new shapes, types, or static arguments. eager execution and captured regions can coexist in one application. JAX’s JIT guide.
see MLIR for multi-level ir enabling progressive lowering.
automatic differentiation
Autograd can compose with JIT compilation. here the gradient transformation is applied before requesting compilation of the resulting function:

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
 
 
def loss_fn(params, x, y):
  pred = params @ x
  return jnp.mean((pred - y) ** 2)
 
 
grad_fn = jax.jit(jax.grad(loss_fn))
 
# differentiates the scalar loss with respect to params
# compiles the gradient computation on its first matching call
for a matrix params and vectors x and y with compatible dimensions, loss_fn returns a scalar mean-squared error. reverse-mode differentiation builds the operations needed for its gradient; compilation can optimize the required forward intermediates and backward computation together. JAX’s differentiation guide explains the scalar-output requirement and default differentiation argument.

a form of reductionism: describe the data with fewer bits by finding the redundancy in it, then store the description instead of the data.
a lossless compressor is an injective map C from strings to bit strings, with a decompressor D such that D(C(x))=x. injectivity already limits what any compressor can do. there are 2^n binary strings of length n, and only 2^n-1 binary strings shorter than n. so no lossless compressor shortens every input. a compressor can leave every input unchanged. if it shortens even one input, it must lengthen some other input. useful compression therefore depends on which data is likely.
the entropy limit
Shannon's source coding theorem says how good that bet can be. for a source that emits independent symbols with distribution p, the entropy
H(X) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x) \log_2 p(x)
is the minimum average number of bits per symbol. no uniquely decodable code can average fewer than H(X) bits per symbol, and long enough blocks of n symbols can be coded with an expected length of nH(X)+o(n) bits. a symbol with probability p(x) ideally costs -\log_2 p(x) bits: likely symbols get short codes, unlikely symbols get long ones.
the theorem is about a source, which is a probability model. a single file has no entropy by itself. for an individual string x, the matching idea is the kolmogorov complexity K(x): the length of the shortest program that prints x. K is incomputable. any real compressor still gives an upper bound: K(x)\leq\lvert C(x)\rvert+c_D, where c_D is the length of the decompressor program. the bound can be very loose. the digits of \pi have a short program, and a general-purpose compressor will not find it.
entropy coders
an entropy coder turns a probability model into bits. three designs matter in practice.

entropy coders
an entropy coder turns a probability model into bits. three designs matter in practice.
huffman coding gives each symbol a prefix-free code word from a binary tree, built by repeatedly merging the two least likely symbols. it minimizes average length among binary prefix codes that encode one source symbol at a time, and its average length \bar\ell satisfies H(X)\leq\bar\ell<H(X)+1. the +1 hurts when one symbol dominates. with p=(0.9,0.1), H\approx0.469 bits, but huffman still spends 1 bit per symbol.
arithmetic coding removes the whole-bit restriction. it narrows an interval inside [0,1) by the probability of each symbol in turn, and outputs enough bits to name a point in the final interval. with exact arithmetic and a known message length, a message x can be encoded in fewer than -\log_2 p(x)+2 bits, so the termination overhead is shared across the message. finite-precision implementations add rounding overhead and must keep the encoder and decoder in sync (witten, neal and cleary, 1987).
asymmetric numeral systems (ans) (Duda, 2013) keep the state in one integer. the frequencies are quantized to integers f_s that sum to M, and B_s=\sum_{t<s}f_t is the start of the range [B_s,B_s+f_s) for symbol s. the range variant (rans) encodes symbol s into state x as
x' = M\left\lfloor \frac{x}{f_s} \right\rfloor + B_s + (x \bmod f_s).
the state grows by a factor of about M/f_s, so \log_2 x grows by about -\log_2(f_s/M) bits, which is the ideal cost of s. to decode, the slot x' \bmod M identifies s, and x = f_s\lfloor x'/M\rfloor + (x' \bmod M) - B_s restores the old state.
a small example with f_a=3, f_b=1, M=4, B_a=0, B_b=3. start at x=10:

encode b: x'=4\cdot10+3+0=43. the state grew by a factor of 43/10=4.3, so \log_2 x increased by about 2.104 bits. the ideal cost is -\log_2(1/4)=2 bits.
encode a: x'=4\cdot14+0+1=57. the state grew by 57/43, so \log_2 x increased by about 0.407 bits. the ideal cost is -\log_2(3/4)\approx0.415 bits.
decode: 57 \bmod 4=1 lies in [0,3), so the symbol is a, and x=3\cdot14+1-0=43. then 43 \bmod 4=3 gives b, and x=1\cdot10+3-3=10.

decoding returns symbols in reverse order, so encoders process the input backward. a real coder also renormalizes: when the state leaves an interval [L,bL), it writes or reads its low bits so the integer stays in a fixed machine width.
tabled ans (tans) distributes symbol slots across a finite state table and precomputes transitions for states in [L,2L), so encoding and decoding become table lookups. this gives arithmetic-coding compression rates at speeds near huffman coding.

how close tans gets 

following Kosolobov (2022), take a string of length n=2^r in which symbol a occurs f_a times, from an alphabet of \sigma symbols. tans with duda’s “precise initialization” encodes it in
\sum_{a} f_a \log_2 \frac{n}{f_a} + O(\sigma + r)
bits, not counting the frequency table. the first term is n times the zero-order empirical entropy. kosolobov gives strings that need the \Omega(\sigma+r) excess. this refutes duda’s conjecture of O(\sigma/n^2) redundancy per symbol: outside the r-bit term, the worst-case excess per symbol is O(\sigma/n), with matching examples when \sigma is proportional to n.

dictionary methods
a la lz77 and zstd
an entropy coder uses the probabilities supplied by its model. a memoryless model misses dependencies between symbols; a context model can use them. dictionary methods represent repeated substrings directly. lz77 (ziv and lempel, 1977) replaces a repeat with a pointer to an earlier copy: a pair (\text{offset},\text{length}) that says “go back this far and copy this many symbols”. the copy may overlap the text it produces. abababab becomes the literals a, b, then (2,6): go back two symbols and copy six, one symbol at a time.
in its asymptotic, growing-window form, lz77 approaches the entropy rate of a stationary ergodic source without knowing that source in advance. for individual strings, consider the greedy parse with unbounded history whose copies lie wholly in the already parsed prefix. its phrase count z is at most the total right-hand-side length of any grammar generating just that string (charikar et al., 2005, lemma 9). this compares phrases with grammar symbols. the number of bits used to store each representation still matters.
zstandard (zstd) parses with an lz77-style matcher, then entropy-codes the results. RFC 8878 specifies huffman coding for literal bytes and fse, a tans implementation, for the literal lengths, match lengths and offsets.
grammar-based compression
a grammar compressor stores a context-free grammar that generates exactly one string: the input. such a grammar is also called a straight-line program. each rule has one right-hand side, and expanding the start symbol reproduces the string. the size of the grammar is the total length of its right-hand sides.
sequitur (Nevill-Manning & Witten, 1997) builds the grammar onlinefor string abcab, sequitur produces: S \to AcA, A \to ab. the digram ab is factored into non-terminal A. in one left-to-right pass, in linear time. it maintains two invariants:

digram uniqueness: no pair of adjacent symbols has two non-overlapping occurrences in the grammar.
rule utility: every rule except the start rule is used at least twice.

rule utility: every rule except the start rule is used at least twice.

when a digram ab appears a second time without overlapping the first, sequitur replaces it with an existing rule for ab, or creates A \to ab and replaces both occurrences. the two copies of aa in aaa overlap, so they produce no rule. when a rule drops to one use, sequitur inlines it.
re-pair (Larsson & Moffat, 1999) works offline. it replaces non-overlapping occurrences of the most frequent pair in the whole string with a new symbol, updates the frequencies, and repeats until no pair has two non-overlapping occurrences. larsson and moffat give an expected linear-time implementation; rescanning the whole string after each replacement would lose that bound (1811.01472⁠ (Sakai et al., 2018) ). it needs the whole input. the greedy choice is a heuristic and does not guarantee the smallest grammar.
finding the smallest grammar is np-hard. polynomial-time algorithms achieve an approximation factor O(1+\log(N/g)), where N is the length of the string and g the size of the smallest grammar (charikar et al., 2005; rytter, 2003). Jeż (2013) reaches this factor in linear time with recompression, assuming an integer alphabet whose symbols fit in O(\log N) bits. it alternates two phases on the current string:

block compression: replace each maximal run a^k with k>1 by a symbol for that run.
pair compression: choose a left-right partition of the alphabet that covers a constant fraction of adjacent pairs. replace each pair ab with a on the left and b on the right by a symbol for that pair. the partition guarantees that these occurrences do not overlap.

equal pairs and equal runs share their replacement symbol. a pair needs one binary grammar rule; a long run needs a subgrammar of binary rules so its expansion is counted in the grammar size. the string shrinks by a constant factor in each round. to obtain the stated approximation bound, the improved algorithm also records the cost of stopping after each round: the rules built so far plus one start rule for the remaining string. it returns the cheapest of these grammars.

transformers keep a key and value vector for every past token. kv compression methods such as h2o and snapkv drop the entries that receive little attention. this is lossy: the bet is that a dropped token will not matter for later queries.

this theorem shares a name with kolmogorov complexity and nothing else. it writes a continuous function of several variables with sums and compositions of one-variable functions. it is a representation result. it says nothing about the length of a description.

Connectionism earns its keep when a representation is a state of a distributed system.
The basic object is a vector of activations:
h = \sigma(Wx + b).
The word “distributed” means that one unit can participate in many concepts and one concept can use many units. A unit is a coordinate. A concept is usually a direction, region, basin, or circuit in activation space. This is why the old grandmother-neuron story is too small for the thing people actually train. The model stores reuse, overlap, interference, and abstraction in the same geometry.
This is the good part of connectionism. It gives an account of how a system can carry structure without a hand-written symbol table.
backprop as credit assignment
Backpropagation is accounting for derivatives through a computation graph. Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams described the useful fact in 1986: hidden units can learn internal features because the training rule sends error information through intermediate layers. (Rumelhart et al., 1986)
For layer \ell:
z^\ell = W^\ell a^{\ell - 1} + b^\ell,
\qquad
a^\ell = \sigma(z^\ell).
For a loss L, the backward pass computes an error signal:
\delta^\ell
  =
  \left((W^{\ell + 1})^\top \delta^{\ell + 1}\right)
  \odot
  \sigma'(z^\ell).
The weight gradient is:
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^\ell}
  =
  \delta^\ell (a^{\ell - 1})^\top.
A first-order update is:
W^\ell
  \leftarrow
  W^\ell
  -
  \eta
  \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^\ell}.
This is local reuse of the chain rule. Claims about what the network represents have to come from the dataset, objective, architecture, optimizer trajectory, and learned state.

Cybenko’s theorem says that finite sums of sigmoids can uniformly approximate continuous scalar functions on a compact subset of \mathbb{R}^n. (Cybenko, 1989)
For a continuous function f: K \to \mathbb{R} on compact K \subset \mathbb{R}^n, and for every \epsilon > 0, there are coefficients \alpha_i, weights w_i, and biases b_i such that:
g(x)
  =
  \sum_{i=1}^{N}
  \alpha_i
  \sigma(w_i^\top x + b_i)
and:
\sup_{x \in K} |f(x) - g(x)| < \epsilon.
Vector outputs follow by approximating each coordinate. The theorem gives an existence result. It leaves training, sample complexity, robustness, semantics, and the behavior of gradient descent open.
The theorem is still important because it tells us the expressivity bottleneck usually moves elsewhere. Once the network is wide enough, the harder questions are data, optimization, inductive bias, and compute.
attractors and memory
Hopfield networks made the connectionist memory story crisp. A binary network state s \in \{-1, 1\}^n evolves until it reaches a stable pattern. With symmetric weights w_{ij} = w_{ji} and no self-connections w_{ii} = 0, one common energy function is: (Hopfield, 1982)
E(s)
  =
  -\frac{1}{2}
  \sum_{i,j}
  w_{ij}s_i s_j
  +
  \sum_i
  \theta_i s_i.
With asynchronous updates under the usual threshold rule, the energy decreases or stays fixed. Memory is a basin of attraction. A corrupted pattern can fall into the stored pattern because the system dynamics make that state stable.

With asynchronous updates under the usual threshold rule, the energy decreases or stays fixed. Memory is a basin of attraction. A corrupted pattern can fall into the stored pattern because the system dynamics make that state stable.
That mechanism matters because it turns recall into dynamics. A memory consists of a region of state space and an update rule that pulls nearby states inward.
tensor product binding
Smolensky’s tensor product representation gives a clean way to write variable binding in a distributed system. (Smolensky, 1990)
Let r_i be a role vector and f_i be a filler vector. A structured representation can bind many role-filler pairs:
T
  =
  \sum_i
  r_i \otimes f_i.
To retrieve the filler for role r_j, contract along the role slot:
\langle r_j, T \rangle_1
  =
  \sum_i
  \langle r_j, r_i \rangle f_i.
If the role vectors are orthonormal, this becomes:
\langle r_j, T \rangle_1 = f_j.
If the role vectors are only approximately orthogonal, retrieval includes cross-talk. That is the honest distributed-representation tradeoff. Capacity comes with interference.
inductive bias as geometry
Architectures choose which patterns are cheap to represent.
A convolutional layer shares weights over spatial positions:
y_{c,u,v}
  =
  \sum_{d,i,j}
  K_{c,d,i,j}
  x_{d,u+i,v+j}.
This makes translation-local structure cheap.
Self-attention makes token-token routing cheap:
\operatorname{Attn}(Q,K,V)
  =
  \operatorname{softmax}
  \left(
    \frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}
  \right)
  V.
This gives the model a learned routing table over context positions. Attention heads, MLP directions, residual streams, and layer normalization then become the actual objects to inspect.

NTK as the lazy limit
The neural tangent kernel is the inner product of parameter gradients:
\Theta_\theta(x, x')
  =
  \nabla_\theta f_\theta(x)^\top
  \nabla_\theta f_\theta(x').
Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler showed that, in an infinite-width limit, the kernel at initialization converges to a deterministic kernel and stays essentially constant during gradient descent. (Jacot et al., 2018)
For training inputs X and targets y, define the residual:
r_t = f_t(X) - y.
In the infinite-width gradient-flow limit:
\frac{d r_t}{dt}
  =
  -\Theta_0(X, X) r_t.
So:
r_t
  =
  \exp\left(-\Theta_0(X, X)t\right) r_0.
This is a boundary case. It describes lazy learning, where features move little and training behaves like kernel regression. Finite networks can learn features. The useful lesson is that width, learning rate, parameterization, and optimizer path decide how close training stays to the NTK regime.
mechanistic interpretability
Mechanistic interpretability tries to reverse-engineer the learned representation. A common move is to fit an overcomplete sparse autoencoder to activations:
h
  =
  \operatorname{ReLU}(W_{\mathrm{enc}}x + b),
\qquad
\hat{x}
  =
  W_{\mathrm{dec}}h + c.
The usual objective is:
\mathcal{L}
  =
  \|x - \hat{x}\|_2^2
  +
  \lambda \|h\|_1.

This can expose sparse directions that look like features. (Elhage et al., 2022) A feature earns its name after causal tests: ablation, activation patching, steering, and prediction of held-out behavior. Naming a direction from examples alone is only a hypothesis.
This is where connectionism becomes an empirical science rather than a vibe. A learned representation is real when changing it changes the model in the predicted way.
the Bitter Lesson
Sutton’s Bitter Lesson says that methods which exploit computation through search and learning tend to win over hand-coded domain structure in the long run. (Sutton, 2019)
For connectionism, the practical reading is:

Put as little ontology into the model as the task permits.
Spend compute on learning the representation.
Inspect the learned representation after training.
Keep hand-coded structure when it buys sample efficiency, stability, or safety.

The last point matters. Inductive bias is still structure. The lesson says to make structure earn its rent under scaling pressure.
boundary conditions
Claims about consciousness require an explicit measure of causal integration and a falsifiable test. A trained neural network supplies weights, activations, losses, and behavior traces. The bridge from those objects to experience remains unbuilt. (Tononi et al., 2016)
Meta-learning and learned optimizers can move part of the update rule inside training. The outer objective, data distribution, compute budget, and selection process still come from outside the system, so recursive self-improvement requires a separate argument.

Searle’s useful split is epistemic objectivity versus ontological subjectivity. A claim is epistemically objective when different observers can settle it by public standards. A thing is ontologically subjective when it exists only as someone having it, e.g. pain or seeing red.
Keep the axes separate. We can study consciousness with public evidence, including neural activity, reports, and behaviour. The experience itself has first-person existence, because pain is pain only for the subject who feels it.
That blocks a sloppy reduction. We can causally reduce a conscious state to neural mechanisms when we explain how the brain produces it. That does not ontologically reduce the experience into a third-person object. The first-person occurrence is still the thing explained.

Content-addressed storage gives an object a key derived from its bytes. In a simple store, the key is k=H(b), where b is the stored byte string and H is a cryptographic hash function.1 To check a retrieved object, hash its bytes and compare the result with the requested key. This checks that the object matches the key; deciding which key to trust is a separate problem.
An ISBN identifies a publication’s title, edition and format. It is assigned through a publishing system, so it cannot verify a downloaded book’s bytes.



Address
What it identifies




Content key
An object encoded with a particular hashing scheme. Its bytes can be checked against the key.


Location, such as a URL used over HTTP
A place to request a resource. The response can change while the URL stays the same.



A hash has a fixed number of possible outputs, so collisions exist. A suitable cryptographic hash makes finding a collision impractical under its security assumptions. It also lets identical encoded objects share a key, which supports deduplication. The key alone provides no storage capacity or availability: some store or peer still has to retain and serve the object.
In IPFS, a CID includes format and hash information. A file may be split into blocks and represented by a DAG, so its root CID generally differs from a hash of the raw file bytes. Chunking and encoding settings affect that root.
Immutable Objects, Mutable References
In a Merkle DAG, nodes contain links to their children by content key. Editing a child changes its key, assuming no collision. Updating the parent’s link then changes the parent’s key, continuing up to the root. Unchanged nodes can be shared between versions. The Merkle DAG structure makes each root identify a particular version.
A mutable reference supplies the name for the latest version. Publish a new root, then update that reference. IPNS uses signed records for this purpose. Readers must verify the reference’s authority and freshness; old content keys still refer to the old objects for as long as those objects remain available.
See also IPFS, Block-reference mechanism

(Yu et al., 2022) replaces request-level batching with iteration-level scheduling: the server rebuilds the batch after every decoding step, so a finished request leaves and a queued one joins without waiting for the rest of its batch. 1
static batching
the naive approach is to form a batch of N requests and run it until ALL of them complete. A request that finishes early keeps its slot and produces padding until the longest one finishes.

time →    t1  t2  t3  t4  t5  t6  t7  t8 │ t9  t10 ...
         ╔═══════════════════════════════╗
 seq A:  ║ ●   ●   ●   ●   ·   ·   ·   · ║  (waiting in queue)
 seq B:  ║ ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ● ║  (waiting in queue)
 seq C:  ║ ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ·   · ║  (waiting in queue)
         ╚═══════════════════════════════╝
         └────── batch 1 locked ─────────┘

 ● = generate token    · = padding (wasted compute)

With output lengths \ell_1,\dots,\ell_N, the batch runs N\max_i \ell_i token slots and only \sum_i \ell_i of them are useful. Above, 3\cdot 8-(4+8+6)=6 of 24 slots are padding, so 25\%. The waste grows with the spread of output lengths, and a new request also waits for the whole batch even when a slot is idle.
iteration-level scheduling
after EACH forward pass (one “iteration”), check which sequences emitted EOS or hit their length limit. Evict them and admit new requests from the queue.

time →   t1  t2  t3  t4  t5  t6  t7  t8  t9  t10
         ├───┼───┼───┼───┼───┼───┼───┼───┼───┼───┤
slot 1:  │ A   A   A   A │ D   D   D   D   D │ F ...
slot 2:  │ B   B   B   B   B   B   B   B │ E   E ...
slot 3:  │ C   C   C   C   C   C │ ← (queue empty)
                         ↑       ↑
                         │       └─ C done, no waiting request
                         └─ A done at t4, D admitted at t5

no slot produces padding after its request ends. This raises throughput and lowers queueing delay. It does not make decoding compute-bound: a decode step reads all weights and each request’s KV cache to produce one token per request, so it is usually limited by memory bandwidth.
selective batching
Iteration-level scheduling creates a batch whose requests sit at different positions. A request in prefill contributes many tokens and a request in decode contributes one. Dense tensors of shape [B, \ell, d] would need padding again. Orca’s answer is selective batching: flatten all tokens of all requests into one [\sum_i n_i, d] matrix for the QKV projections, output projection and MLP, because those operations treat each token independently. Attention is split per request, because each token attends only to its own request’s keys and values. (Yu et al., 2022)
single iteration
each iteration runs:

┌─────────────────── iteration t ───────────────────┐
│                                                   │
│  1. prefill: new request D (n prompt tokens)      │
│     ┌──────────────────────────────┐              │
│     │ prompt tokens → Q,K,V proj   │  O(n) tokens │
│     │ → causal attention           │  O(n²)       │
│     │ → write K,V to cache         │              │
│     └──────────────────────────────┘              │
│                                                   │
│  2. decode: existing A,B,C                        │
│     ┌──────────────────────────────┐              │
│     │ last token → Q,K,V proj      │  1 token/seq │
│     │ read K,V cache → attention   │  O(seq_len)  │
│     │ → output proj → next token   │              │
│     └──────────────────────────────┘              │
│                                                   │
│  3. sample: argmax/nucleus per sequence           │
│                                                   │
│  4. check: A hit EOS → evict, free KV cache       │
│                                                   │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

mixing a long prefill into the same iteration makes that step slow for every decoding request in it. Splitting long prompts into chunks bounds that stall; see PD disaggregated serving for the separation of the two phases.
the binding constraint is KV-cache memory. Each token stores a key and a value vector at every layer:
\text{bytes per token} = 2 \cdot L \cdot n_{\text{kv}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot b,
with L layers, n_{\text{kv}} key/value heads, head size d_{\text{head}} and b bytes per element. For OPT-13B in fp16 (L=40, n_{\text{kv}}d_{\text{head}}=5120, b=2) this is 819{,}200 bytes, about 800 KB per token, so one 2048-token sequence holds about 1.7 GB. (Kwon et al., 2023) The number of concurrent requests is bounded by the cache memory divided by the per-request footprint.
KV cache fragmentation
Fragmentation comes from how the cache is allocated, independent of the batching policy. Orca and FasterTransformer reserve one contiguous region per request, sized for the request’s maximum possible length. (Kwon et al., 2023) measured that only 20.4\% to 38.2\% of the KV-cache memory in such systems held actual token states.
internal fragmentation: the region is sized for the maximum length, but the request stops earlier, so the tail of its own region stays unused.

GPU memory for KV cache (max_seq_len = 2048 per slot):
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ seq A: [████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] │
│        used: 512        wasted: 1536 (75%)               │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ seq B: [████████████████████████████████████████████████]│
│        used: 2048       wasted: 0                        │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ seq C: [████████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] │
│        used: 768        wasted: 1280 (63%)               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

there is also reservation waste: a running request holds slots for tokens it has not generated yet.
external fragmentation: requests reserve regions of different sizes, so freed regions leave gaps of different sizes between live ones.

A reserved 512 tokens, C reserved 768, B is still running between them.
After A and C finish, D arrives and needs a 1024-token region:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [ hole: 512 ][███ seq B running ███][ hole: 768 ][ ... ] │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  512 + 768 = 1280 ≥ 1024 tokens are free in total, but no
  single hole holds 1024 contiguous tokens, so D must wait
  for B to finish or for the allocator to compact memory

PagedAttention removes the contiguity requirement. The cache is split into fixed-size blocks (for example 16 tokens), and a per-request block table maps logical positions to physical blocks. A request allocates a new block only when its last block is full, so the waste per request is less than one block and any free block can serve any request. (Kwon et al., 2023)

continuous batching \neq solving memory fragmentation

iteration-level scheduling removes padding slots, but KV-cache fragmentation persists unless the cache is also paged. vLLM combines both.

throughput gains
Orca reported a 36.9\times throughput improvement over NVIDIA FasterTransformer at the same latency, on GPT-3 175B. (Yu et al., 2022) That comparison bundles iteration-level scheduling with selective batching and Orca’s distributed execution, so it does not isolate the scheduling change. vLLM then reported 2 to 4\times higher throughput than FasterTransformer and Orca at the same latency, which measures what paging adds on top of continuous batching. (Kwon et al., 2023) The gain on a given deployment depends on the spread of output lengths, the arrival rate and the memory left for the KV cache.

A set C is convex when the line segment between any two of its points stays inside C:
x,y\in C,\quad t\in[0,1]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(1-t)x+ty\in C.
The segment includes both endpoints and can reduce to a single point when x=y. Convex sets can also be unbounded: a line, a ray and the whole space are examples.1
For a function, look at the line segment joining two points on its graph. Convexity requires the graph to lie on or below that segment between the two inputs.

Definition 1. formal definition 

Let X be a convex subset of a real vector space. A function f:X\to\mathbb{R} is convex if, for every x,y\in X and t\in[0,1],
f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y).
It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct x,y and 0<t<1. Reversing the inequality defines a concave function.

Definition 1. formal definition 

Let X be a convex subset of a real vector space. A function f:X\to\mathbb{R} is convex if, for every x,y\in X and t\in[0,1],
f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y).
It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct x,y and 0<t<1. Reversing the inequality defines a concave function.


For f(x)=x^2, the graph lies below each chord. The same definition includes f(x)=|x|, which has a corner, and affine functions f(x)=ax+b, which satisfy equality everywhere. The cup-shaped picture only covers some examples. Equivalently, f is convex exactly when its epigraph is a convex set.2
derivatives and minima
For differentiable f on an open convex domain in \mathbb{R}^d, convexity is equivalent to
f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)
\qquad\text{for all }x,y\text{ in the domain}.
The tangent approximation gives a lower bound everywhere. If \nabla f(x)=0, this inequality becomes f(y)\ge f(x), so x is a global minimizer. More generally, every local minimum of a convex function is global. Convexity still allows several minimizers or none at all: a constant function attains its minimum everywhere; e^x on \mathbb{R} never reaches its infimum zero.2
Jensen’s inequality
The defining inequality extends from two inputs to a weighted average:
f\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i x_i\right)
\le\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i f(x_i),
\qquad p_i\ge0,\quad\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i=1.

probability theory 

For an integrable real random variable Z taking values in an interval I, and a convex function \varphi:I\to\mathbb{R}, Jensen’s inequality gives
\varphi(\mathbb{E}[Z])\le\mathbb{E}[\varphi(Z)],
provided \mathbb{E}[Z]\in I and \mathbb{E}[|\varphi(Z)|]<\infty.

For example, applying it to \varphi(z)=z^2 gives (\mathbb{E}[Z])^2\le\mathbb{E}[Z^2] when the second moment is finite. The gap is the variance.3
convex hull
The convex hull of a nonempty set \mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d consists of all finite convex combinations of its points:
\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal{X})
=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\theta_i x_i
\;\middle|\;
 m\ge1,\ x_i\in\mathcal{X},\ \theta_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}\theta_i=1\right\}.
Every convex set containing \mathcal{X} must contain these combinations. They form a convex set themselves, so the hull is the smallest convex set containing \mathcal{X}. This also makes it the intersection of all convex sets containing \mathcal{X}.1
Three noncollinear points in the plane have a filled triangle as their hull, including its edges. Three collinear points produce the segment between the two extreme points.
simplex
A k-simplex is the convex hull of k+1 affinely independent vertices u_0,\ldots,u_k. Affine independence means the vectors u_1-u_0,\ldots,u_k-u_0 are linearly independent; it ensures the hull has dimension k.
C=\left\{\sum_{i=0}^{k}\theta_i u_i
\;\middle|\;\theta_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=0}^{k}\theta_i=1\right\}.
The first examples are a point, a line segment, a filled triangle, a tetrahedron and, in four dimensions, a 5-cell. Affine independence matters: the three collinear points above cannot define a 2-simplex.
The probability simplex is a useful instance:
\Delta^{n-1}=\left\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\;\middle|\;p_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i=1\right\}.
Its vertices are the standard basis vectors. Each point represents a distribution over n outcomes; the sum constraint leaves n-1 dimensions.1

Cosine similarity measures how closely two nonzero vectors point in the same direction. Dividing by their lengths removes magnitude from the score, so a vector and a positive multiple of it have similarity 1.

definition 

For x,y\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}, use the Euclidean inner product and norm:
S_C(x,y)=\frac{x^{\mathsf T}y}{\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2}
=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2}}
=\cos\theta.


Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the score to [-1,1]. The endpoints mean the vectors point in the same or opposite directions; a score of 0 means they are orthogonal. A zero vector has no direction, and the formula is undefined for it.
For example, (1,2) and (2,4) have similarity 1 despite their different lengths. In document retrieval, this normalization allows term-frequency vectors from documents of different lengths to be compared by direction. The choice of features still determines what that direction means. Manning, Raghavan, and Schütze, §6.3.1.
relation to correlation
Pearson correlation subtracts each vector’s mean first. For nonconstant real data vectors, its formula is
r(x,y)=S_C\bigl(x-\bar x\mathbf 1,\;y-\bar y\mathbf 1\bigr).
This follows by substituting the centered vectors into the cosine formula. Adding a constant to every coordinate leaves Pearson correlation unchanged and can change cosine similarity. Constant nonzero vectors therefore have a defined cosine similarity even though their Pearson correlation is undefined. See the NIST correlation and cosine formulas.

elements

Definition 1. alphabet 

An alphabet \Sigma is a finite set of symbols, for example \Sigma=\{0,1\}.

A string is a finite sequence of symbols from the alphabet. Over \{0,1\}, 011011 is a string of length 6. An unending sequence of bits is outside this definition.
The empty string \epsilon has length 0. It contains no symbols; it is different from the empty set. For \Sigma=\{a,b\}:
\lvert aaba\rvert=4,\qquad \lvert a^3\rvert=\lvert aaa\rvert=3.
set of string
\Sigma^n is the set of strings of length n. In particular, \Sigma^0=\{\epsilon\}. The set of all finite strings is
\Sigma^*=\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}\Sigma^n.
If \Sigma has at least one symbol, \Sigma^* is infinite, although each of its strings is finite. Allowing an empty alphabet gives \varnothing^*=\{\epsilon\}. The empty string is always in \Sigma^*; it is not an input symbol. These are the alphabet, string and language conventions in Western’s automata notes.
concatenation
Concatenation appends one string to another: x=101 and y=111 give xy=101111.
\begin{aligned}
x^0&=\epsilon, & x^n&=xx^{n-1}\quad(n\geq1),\\
(xy)z&=x(yz), & \lvert xy\rvert&=\lvert x\rvert+\lvert y\rvert,\\
\epsilon x&=x\epsilon=x.
\end{aligned}
language
A language over \Sigma is any subset L\subseteq\Sigma^*. It need not come with a procedure for deciding membership. For languages over the same alphabet:
\begin{aligned}
\overline L&=\Sigma^*\setminus L,\\
L_1L_2&=\{xy\mid x\in L_1,\ y\in L_2\},\\
L^0&=\{\epsilon\},\qquad L^n=LL^{n-1}\quad(n\geq1),\\
L^*&=\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}L^n.
\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}
\overline L&=\Sigma^*\setminus L,\\
L_1L_2&=\{xy\mid x\in L_1,\ y\in L_2\},\\
L^0&=\{\epsilon\},\qquad L^n=LL^{n-1}\quad(n\geq1),\\
L^*&=\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}L^n.
\end{aligned}
Union and intersection have their usual set meanings. Complement depends on the alphabet: changing \Sigma changes the strings outside L.
definition
A deterministic finite automaton is
\begin{aligned}
M&=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,s,F),\\
Q&:\text{finite, nonempty set of states},\\
\Sigma&:\text{finite input alphabet},\\
\delta&:Q\times\Sigma\to Q,\\
s&\in Q,\qquad F\subseteq Q.
\end{aligned}
Here \delta is total: every state has exactly one next state for each input symbol. If a diagram omits an impossible input, complete it with a rejecting sink whose transitions return to itself. The current state is the machine’s entire memory of the prefix it has read. Cornell’s DFA definition uses this total-transition convention.
examples
Over \Sigma=\{a,b\}, accept strings containing at least three occurrences of a. Use
Q=\{s_1,s_2,s_3,s_4\},\qquad s=s_1,\qquad F=\{s_4\}.
States s_1,s_2,s_3 mean that the prefix contains respectively zero, one or two occurrences of a. State s_4 means at least three. Once that threshold is reached, the exact count cannot affect acceptance.

Stateab\to s_1s_2s_1s_2s_3s_2s_3s_4s_3*s_4s_4s_4
The incoming arrow marks the start; an asterisk marks acceptance. The table is a representation of \delta. Reading b leaves the count unchanged, and reading a increments it until the saturated state s_4. For example, ababa is accepted and abbab is rejected. Acceptance is checked after the whole input.
language.
The language recognized by M is a set of strings, so \mathcal L(M)\subseteq\Sigma^*. To express it, extend the one-symbol transition function to whole strings.
transfer function
\begin{aligned}
\delta &:Q\times\Sigma\to Q,\\
\hat\delta &:Q\times\Sigma^*\to Q,\\
\hat\delta(q,\epsilon)&=q,\\
\hat\delta(q,xa)&=\delta(\hat\delta(q,x),a)
\quad(x\in\Sigma^*,\ a\in\Sigma).
\end{aligned}
The recursive rule processes the prefix x, then reads a. The finite table for \delta therefore determines the result for every finite input.

acceptance
M\text{ accepts }x\iff\hat\delta(s,x)\in F,\qquad
\mathcal L(M)=\{x\in\Sigma^*\mid\hat\delta(s,x)\in F\}.
Visiting an accepting state midway through a run does not settle the result. The suffix-ab machine accepts ab and rejects aba. The empty string is accepted exactly when s\in F. See Cornell’s language-of-a-machine notes.
For binary strings representing a multiple of three or the number six, six adds no accepted number because it is already a multiple of three. A remainder machine suffices:
\delta(r,b)=(2r+b)\bmod3,\qquad r\in\{0,1,2\},\quad b\in\{0,1\}.
Appending a binary digit doubles the old value and adds the digit. Start in remainder 0 and accept remainder 0. This version also accepts \epsilon. If the exercise requires a nonempty numeral, add a rejecting start state with the same outgoing transitions as remainder 0.
regular
A language is regular when some DFA recognizes exactly that language. Some useful cases:

\{a^n\mid n\geq0\} and \{a^nb^m\mid n,m\geq0\} are regular. They require tracking which symbols are allowed next.
\{a^nb^n\mid0\leq n\leq3\} is finite and regular. A DFA can track prefixes of its four strings and reject every other continuation.
\{a^nb^n\mid n\geq0\} is nonregular. Suppose a DFA had k states. Two of the k+1 prefixes \epsilon,a,\ldots,a^k must reach the same state, say a^i and a^j with i<j. Appending b^i would then give the same verdict for both, although only a^ib^i belongs to the language. This contradicts recognition.

The same prefixes distinguish strings for \{x\mid\#_a(x)=\#_b(x)\}, where \#_a(x) counts occurrences of a. A regular language can therefore have nonregular subsets: \{a^nb^n\mid n\geq0\}\subseteq\{a^nb^m\mid n,m\geq0\}. Passing to an NFA does not change which languages are regular. Stanford’s Myhill–Nerode guide develops this distinguishing-suffix argument.
For regular languages over the same alphabet, complement, intersection and union are regular.
proof (1)
For a complete DFA M=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,s,F), replace F with Q\setminus F. Every input has exactly one completed run, whose verdict is reversed:
\mathcal L(Q,\Sigma,\delta,s,Q\setminus F)=\Sigma^*\setminus\mathcal L(M).
Completeness matters. A missing transition must lead to a sink before complementing, because an input rejected by getting stuck must become accepted.
proof (2)
Let M_1 and M_2 recognize L_1 and L_2. Run both machines on the same input and store the pair of current states. For every prefix x:
\hat\delta_\times((p,q),x)=
(\hat\delta_1(p,x),\hat\delta_2(q,x)).
Induction on the length of x proves this: the empty input leaves both coordinates unchanged, and each next symbol updates both once. Accepting only pairs whose two coordinates accept gives L_1\cap L_2. Accepting pairs with at least one accepting coordinate gives L_1\cup L_2.
product construction
The shared transition structure is
\begin{aligned}
Q_\times&=Q_1\times Q_2,\qquad s_\times=(s_1,s_2),\\
\delta_\times((p,q),a)&=(\delta_1(p,a),\delta_2(q,a)).
\end{aligned}
The accepting sets differ:
\begin{aligned}
F_\cap&=F_1\times F_2,\\
F_\cup&=(F_1\times Q_2)\cup(Q_1\times F_2)\\

Only e_0 accepts. For instance, 110 represents 6 and ends in e_0. The strings 11 and 10 represent 3 and 2; they would pass the union test, while the intersection rejects both.
quotient construction
lec feb 4
Two states are equivalent when every possible remaining input gives the same acceptance verdict:
p\approx q\iff\forall x\in\Sigma^*:
\bigl(\hat\delta(p,x)\in F\iff\hat\delta(q,x)\in F\bigr).
Taking x=\epsilon shows that equivalent states agree on acceptance. They also satisfy the right-congruence condition
p\approx q\implies\delta(p,a)\approx\delta(q,a)
\quad\text{for every }a\in\Sigma.
Otherwise a distinguishing suffix after a would distinguish p and q as well. Define [p]=\{q\in Q\mid p\approx q\}. Then [p]=[q] exactly when p\approx q. The quotient DFA is
\begin{aligned}
Q'&=\{[p]\mid p\in Q\},\\
\delta'([p],a)&=[\delta(p,a)],\\
s'&=[s],\qquad F'=\{[p]\mid p\in F\}.
\end{aligned}
Right congruence makes the transition independent of the representative chosen from a class. Agreement on acceptance makes F' well-defined. Remove unreachable states first; quotienting the reachable states by this equivalence gives a minimal DFA.
For the product table above, the classes are
A=\{e_0\},\quad B=\{o_0\},\quad
C=\{e_1,o_1\},\quad D=\{e_2,o_2\}.

State01*AAC\to BACCDBDCD
States A and B have identical outgoing transitions, yet differ on the empty suffix. State B differs from C and D on suffix 0; C differs from D on suffix 10. All four classes are reachable, so the quotient is minimal.
To find the classes by table filling:

List unordered pairs of distinct reachable states.
Mark each pair with exactly one accepting state. The empty suffix distinguishes it.
Mark an unmarked pair if some symbol leads to a marked pair.
Repeat step 3 until a whole pass adds no marks. Only then merge the unmarked pairs.

Each propagated mark has a distinguishing suffix: prepend the transition symbol to the suffix that distinguished its successors. At the fixed point, unmarked pairs agree on acceptance and their successors remain unmarked, so induction gives agreement for every suffix. See Cornell’s minimization notes.

This is essentially two stages for training and inference (MHA and MQA respectively)
standard MHA projects inputs to d-dimensional vectors, then splits them into h heads.
kv cache size per token would be n_{\text{heads}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times 2 (for KV).
training mode (MHA-style)
during training, we need gradients to flow through distinct up-projections to learn head-specific features.
k_t = c_{KV} W_{UK}
v_t = c_{KV} W_{UV}
A = \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{q_t (c_{KV} W_{UK})^T}{\sqrt{d}}\right) (c_{KV} W_{UV})
This makes sense given that we require full rank MHA for activations fully materialized.
inference mode (MQA-style)
Associativity of matrix multiplication allows us to merge the up-projection W_{UK} into the query projection W_{Q}.
recall that A \propto q k^T.
if we expand k:
\text{score} = q_t (c_{KV} W_{UK})^T = q_t W_{UK}^T c_{KV}^T
notice we can group (q_t W_{UK}^T). let’s define an absorbed query:
Q_{\text{absorbed}} = Q_{\text{original}} \cdot W_{UK}^T
now the attention score is:
\text{score} = Q_{\text{absorbed}} \cdot c_{KV}^T
Now, we never have compute/store the full high-dim key matrix K during inference. And we only store the tiny compressed latent c_{KV}, which is nice

  k_pe, k_nope = torch.split(

  )

  k_pe = apply_rotary_emb(k_pe.unsqueeze(2), freqs_cis, False).squeeze(2)
  k = torch.cat([k_pe, k_nope], dim=-1)
  q = rotate_activation(q)
  k = rotate_activation(k)
  q_fp8, q_scale = act_quant(q, block_size, self.scale_fmt)
  k_fp8, k_scale = act_quant(k, block_size, self.scale_fmt)
  self.k_cache[:bsz, start_pos:end_pos] = k_fp8
  self.k_scale_cache[:bsz, start_pos:end_pos] = k_scale
  weights = self.weights_proj(x.float()) * self.n_heads**-0.5
  weights = weights.unsqueeze(-1) * q_scale * self.softmax_scale
  index_score = fp8_index(
    q_fp8.contiguous(),
    weights,
    self.k_cache[:bsz, :end_pos].contiguous(),
    self.k_scale_cache[:bsz, :end_pos].contiguous(),
  )
  if mask is not None:
    index_score += mask

self.k_scale_cache[:bsz, start_pos:end_pos] = k_scale
  weights = self.weights_proj(x.float()) * self.n_heads**-0.5
  weights = weights.unsqueeze(-1) * q_scale * self.softmax_scale
  index_score = fp8_index(
    q_fp8.contiguous(),
    weights,
    self.k_cache[:bsz, :end_pos].contiguous(),
    self.k_scale_cache[:bsz, :end_pos].contiguous(),
  )
  if mask is not None:
    index_score += mask
  topk_indices = index_score.topk(min(self.index_topk, end_pos), dim=-1)[1]
  topk_indices_ = topk_indices.clone()
  dist.broadcast(topk_indices_, src=0)

R1 training, distillation, and V3’s compute and memory costs.
R1 explores inference-time compute: a model can spend more tokens working through a problem before answering. Its training starts from DeepSeek-V3-Base, which already contains the capabilities learned during pretraining.
Three experiments to keep separate:

R1-Zero applies reinforcement learning directly to that base checkpoint, without a supervised fine-tuning warmup.
R1 combines two supervised fine-tuning stages with two RL stages.
R1 Distill transfers generated examples to smaller Qwen and Llama models through knowledge distillation.

The 2501.12948⁠ (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025)  describes the January 2025 models. The V3.1 and V3.2-Exp sections below concern later releases.
R1-Zero
GRPO, introduced in DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024), compares rewards among answers sampled for the same prompt. This gives each sampled answer an advantage estimate without training a separate critic.
Group-Relative-Policy-Optimization 
R1-Zero uses rule-based accuracy rewards, such as checking a mathematical answer or running code against test cases. It also rewards the required reasoning format. The prompt already asks for reasoning followed by an answer; self-correction strategies are left unspecified.
During RL, responses grow longer and include revisiting earlier steps. The report’s “aha moment” is one such generated example. This supports a claim about learned output behaviour. Whether those words faithfully describe the computation needs a separate experiment.
Poor readability and language mixing remain problems. Explaining the choice of language would require evidence about the tokenizer, training distribution, and rewards. The starting checkpoint matters here: RL is selecting among behaviours a pretrained model can already generate.
R1
stage 1: cold start
Fine-tune V3-Base on thousands of readable long-CoT examples, including processed R1-Zero outputs. This supplies both examples and an output structure before RL. Assigning its entire effect to formatting would require an ablation.
stage 2: reasoning-oriented RL
Train on verifiable reasoning tasks. Add a language-consistency reward to accuracy; the authors report a small performance cost for this readability constraint.
stage 3: rejection sampling and supervised fine-tuning
Sample the RL checkpoint and retain correct, readable responses. Combine roughly 600,000 reasoning examples with 200,000 general-task examples, then fine-tune V3-Base for two epochs. This stage trains the full-size R1 pipeline and supplies the dataset later used for distillation.
stage 4: all-scenario RL
Combine rule-based reasoning rewards with learned preference rewards for general tasks. Helpfulness is judged on the final answer; harmlessness is judged on the whole response. (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025)

These results concern particular tasks and sampling settings. They leave instruction following, reliability, and deployment latency to be tested separately. Distill
process
The released dense models have 1.5B, 7B, 8B, 14B, 32B, and 70B parameters. They start from Qwen2.5 or Llama checkpoints and receive supervised fine-tuning on the roughly 800,000-example dataset above. The reported distillation run adds no RL stage.
distillation objectives
The student learns to predict the teacher’s sampled text. For a prompt q and target response y, the usual supervised objective is
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)
= -\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}\log p_\theta(y_t\mid q,y_{<t}).
This transfers a sequence of attempted steps and an answer. It gives the student more tokens to learn from than an answer-only target. Establishing which parts cause the gain requires controlling for prompt selection, correctness filtering, response length, and training compute.

results
In the original distilled-model evaluation, R1-Distill-Qwen-7B scores 55.5% on AIME 2024 and 92.8% on MATH-500. The same table reports 9.3% and 74.6% for GPT-4o-0513. On GPQA Diamond, the 7B model scores 49.1% against GPT-4o’s 49.9%. The gains vary by task.
Total parameter count alone cannot give an inference speedup. R1 activates about 37B of its 671B parameters per token; the distilled models are dense. Hardware, weight placement, batch size, and generated token count all affect latency.
open source release
The official repository provides the report and links to model weights. It does not provide the complete R1 training pipeline or the curated 800,000-example dataset. Open-R1 is a separate community reproduction effort. Released weights allow local inference and further training; exact reproduction also needs the missing data and training details.
DeepSeek-V3
671B total parameters, about 37B activated per token, pretrained on 14.8T tokens. The 2412.19437⁠ (DeepSeek-AI, Liu, et al., 2025)  separates model architecture, numerical precision, and distributed execution. Each changes a different part of the resource bill.
architecture
Multi-head Latent Attention caches a compressed joint key/value representation plus a separate rotary-position key. V3 uses 512 dimensions for the latent and 64 for the rotary key, giving 512+64=576 cached scalars per token per layer before storage overhead. The decoder can reuse this compact state for every generated token.

architecture
Multi-head Latent Attention caches a compressed joint key/value representation plus a separate rotary-position key. V3 uses 512 dimensions for the latent and 64 for the rotary key, giving 512+64=576 cached scalars per token per layer before storage overhead. The decoder can reuse this compact state for every generated token.
The first three layers use dense feed-forward networks. Each later MoE layer has one shared expert and 256 routed experts, with eight routed experts selected per token. The shared expert processes every token; routed computation permits a larger set of weights without evaluating all of them for each token.
multi-token prediction
V3 trains with one additional prediction depth, D=1. The main model predicts the next token; a further Transformer module combines its hidden representation with the next token’s embedding to predict the token after that. During training, that embedding comes from the observed sequence.
For D additional depths, the auxiliary objective is
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MTP}}
= \frac{\lambda}{D}\sum_{k=1}^{D}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MTP}}^{k},
where each \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MTP}}^{k} is cross-entropy on the corresponding future-token targets. The modules share the main model’s embedding and output head and preserve a causal chain through the intervening tokens. This differs from attaching independent prediction heads to a single hidden state. At inference, the extra module can be removed or used for speculative decoding. (DeepSeek-AI, Liu, et al., 2025)
Transformers #multi-token-prediction
training optimizations
DualPipe overlaps forward/backward computation with expert dispatch, expert-result collection, and pipeline communication. Its schedule reduces idle pipeline time, with some bubbles remaining at the beginning and end of the pipeline.
FP8 mixed precision uses E4M3 for the FP8 tensors in forward and backward matrix multiplications. Scaling is fine-grained: activation tiles of 1\times128 elements and weight blocks of 128\times128. Master weights and gradient accumulation remain FP32, with other sensitive operations retained at higher precision. “FP8 training” names part of the numerical pipeline.
Communication uses InfiniBand across nodes and NVLink within a node. Routing limits how many nodes each token visits. Overlap can hide transfers only while useful computation is available to run alongside them; the network still carries the bytes.

training efficiency
The report’s compute accounting assumes $2 per H800 GPU-hour:

StageH800 GPU-hoursPretraining2,664,000Context extension119,000Post-training5,000Total2,788,000
This gives the quoted $5.576M for the reported V3 run. Earlier architecture experiments, ablations, and data research are excluded. It also says nothing about the total cost of developing R1. Comparing this figure with another lab’s full development budget would mix accounting boundaries.
load balancing without auxiliary loss
For expert i and token t, let s_{i,t} be the router’s affinity score. V3 selects experts using
S_t=\operatorname{TopK}_{i}(s_{i,t}+b_i).
The bias b_i affects selection. The mixture weights still come from the original scores s_{i,t}. After a training step, the router decreases an overloaded expert’s bias by \gamma and increases an underloaded expert’s bias by \gamma, using load measured across the batch. This makes a busy expert less likely to receive the next tokens without adding that pressure to the language-model gradient.
V3 also retains a small sequence-wise auxiliary balancing loss to discourage extreme imbalance within one sequence. Both its coefficient and the bias update speed are hyperparameters.
benchmark performance
The V3 chat-model evaluation reports 88.5% on MMLU, 90.2% on MATH-500, and 59.1% on GPQA Diamond. Keep the model version, dataset subset, and metric with each score. A MATH-500 score cannot be relabelled as a result on the full MATH test set. (DeepSeek-AI, Liu, et al., 2025)

Notes from Carl Hoefer’s Causal Determinism⁠ entry in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
causal

Causal determinism is, roughly speaking, the idea that every event is necessitated by antecedent events and conditions together with the laws of nature.

Stated as a property of a world: if two possible worlds obey the same laws and agree completely at one time, they agree at every later time. The idea is ancient. It first received clarification and mathematical analysis in the eighteenth century, when Laplace imagined an intellect that knew every position and force at one instant and could compute the whole future from them.
Hoefer notes two places where determinism matters. One is physics and its explanatory ambitions. The other is human free action, which ties it to agency. In both, there is no agreement over whether determinism is true, or over what it would mean for agency in either caseor even whether it can be known true or false.
determinism is not predictability
Determinism is a claim about the world. Predictability is a claim about what we can compute from what we can measure. The two come apart. In a chaotic system such as the Lorenz equations, the future is fixed by the present state, but a small error in measuring that state grows exponentially. So the prediction fails after a finite horizon, while the system stays deterministic. Laplace’s intellect needs infinite precision, and we do not have it.
nominative determinism
A different and humorous use of the word, named in New Scientist’s Feedback column in 1994:

people tend to gravitate towards areas of work or interest that fit their name.

It has no connection to causal determinism, apart from the name.

A digital garden is a collection of linked notes that stay open to revision. A note can begin with a question or an excerpt. Later, it can acquire an explanation, a worked example, or a correction. Keeping these changes on the same page gives the idea an address that other notes can refer to. Maggie Appleton’s account describes this practice of publishing unfinished work and revisiting it.
The links make this a form of hypertext. They also need context: a sentence around a link can say whether its target supplies a definition, evidence, or an objection. Wikipedia is a familiar example of linked, revisable pages. A personal garden leaves the selection and interpretation with its author.
Ted Nelson’s Xanadu has further requirements, including durable connections to quoted material and a system for paying rightsholders. Calling any collection of linked notes a Xanadu system would skip those commitments. Nelson’s own explanation draws out the distinction.
Joel Hooks describes the maintenance implied by the name:

A garden is usually a place where things grow.
Gardens can be very personal and full of whimsy or a garden can be a source of food and substance.
We gather and work together in community gardens to share the labor as well as the rewards of a collective effort.
It’s a comparison that you can take very far. From “planting seeds” and “pulling weeds” to tending multiple gardens that each serve an individual need or desired outcome.
Like with real gardens, our digital gardens are a constant ebb and flow towards entropy.

definition

Abstract 

A Dirac measure is a measure \delta_x on a set X (with any \sigma-algebra of subsets of X) defined for a given x \in X and any (measurable) set A \subseteq X by
\delta_x(A) = 1_A(x) = \begin{cases}0, & x \notin A \\ 1, & x \in A\end{cases}


where 1_A is the indicator function of A The Dirac measure is a probability measure, and in terms of probability it represents the almost sure outcome x in the sample space X.We can also say that the measure is a single atom at x. The Dirac measures are the extreme points of the convex set of probability measures on X.
The name is a back-formation from the Dirac delta function; considered as a Schwartz distribution, for example on the real line, measures can be taken to be a special kind of distribution. The identity
\int_X f(y) \, d\delta_x(y) = f(x),
which, in the form
\int_X f(y) \delta_x(y) \, dy = f(x),
is often taken to be part of the definition of the “delta function”, holds as a theorem of Lebesgue integration.
properties
Let \delta_x denote the Dirac measure centred on some fixed point x in some measurable space (X, \Sigma).

\delta_x is a probability measure, and hence a finite measure.

Suppose that (X, T) is a topological space and that \Sigma is at least as fine as the Borel \sigma-algebra \sigma(T) on X.

\delta_x is a strictly positive measure if and only if the topology T is such that x lies within every non-empty open set

e.g. in the case of the trivial topology \{\emptyset, X\}

If X is a Hausdorff topological space with its Borel \sigma-algebra, then \delta_x satisfies the condition to be an inner regular measure, since singleton sets such as \{x\} are always compact. Hence, \delta_x is also a Radon measure \boxed{}.

A Dyson sphere is a hypothetical system for collecting a substantial fraction of a star’s light. A Dyson swarm does this with many collectors in separate orbits. In his 1960 reply, Dyson clarified that this was the arrangement he meant. A rigid shell has separate structural and stability problems (Wright, 2020).
For a star with luminosity L_\star, collectors that absorb a fraction f of its light receive
P_{\mathrm{abs}}=fL_\star.
If the collectors convert a fraction \eta of that input to useful work, useful power is \eta fL_\star. Absorbed fraction and conversion efficiency are separate quantities. A swarm can grow by adding collectors, harvesting power while leaving most of the star uncovered. Collecting nearly the full stellar output gives the physical example behind Type II on the Kardashev scale.
where the energy goes
If all the absorbed energy eventually becomes heat within the system, then at steady state it must radiate that energy away. For radiators at a common temperature T, with emissivity \epsilon and total emitting area A, the heat balance is
fL_\star=\epsilon\sigma A T^4,
\qquad
T=\left(\frac{fL_\star}{\epsilon\sigma A}\right)^{1/4},
where \sigma is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. The model assumes a negligible background temperature and that the emitted heat escapes. Exporting energy in beams or storing it changes the balance; useful work that dissipates locally still becomes heat.
For fixed absorbed power and emissivity, doubling radiator area multiplies temperature by 2^{-1/4}\approx0.84. Halving the temperature takes sixteen times the area.
At temperatures of a few hundred kelvin, the radiators emit mainly in the infrared. Dyson’s original proposal was to search for that emission. Warm dust emits infrared too, so an infrared excess needs follow-up observations before it can support an artificial origin.bibliographieWright, J. T. (2020). Dyson Spheres. Emotion regulation includes noticing and understanding a feeling, accepting that it is present, and choosing how to act while feeling it. Dysregulation can involve difficulty with any of these abilities, including following through on a goal when distressed. Gratz and Roemer’s account gives us a way to describe those difficulties. A moment of anxiety alone gives us too little information to infer a disorder or a brain mechanism.
An unanswered message is an observation. Rejection is one possible explanation for it. The uncertainty matters: treating that explanation as settled adds a claim that the message history may not support.
Naming an emotion is called affect labeling. In a 2007 fMRI experiment, participants labeling emotional images showed lower amygdala activity and higher activity in the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex than during comparison tasks. These measurements describe differences between tasks. They do not establish that naming a feeling switches reasoning back on or reliably relieves everyday anxiety.

Questions to try while the explanation is still uncertain:

In LLMs, a token embedding is a learned table lookup. Let the vocabulary contain m tokens and the model have width d. For token ID u_{b,t} at position t in batch item b:
E\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d},\qquad x_{b,t}=E[u_{b,t},:]\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
The ID selects a row. Two occurrences of the same token start with the same vector; attention later lets their representations depend on their different contexts. The lookup is equivalent to multiplying a one-hot row vector by E, without allocating the one-hot vector. See the embedding operation.
Position enters according to the architecture. An additive scheme uses x_{b,t}+p_t; the original Transformer also scales the token vector by \sqrt d (Vaswani et al., 2023). RoPE applies position-dependent rotations to attention queries and keys, so adding a position vector to every input is not a universal step. The RoFormer derivation shows how these rotations make the query–key dot product depend on relative position (Su et al., 2023).
tokenization and vocab
BPE and WordPiece produce IDs before the embedding lookup. The tokenizer defines which special tokens exist and when to insert them. BOS, EOS, PAD, and UNK are possible vocabulary entries; a model need not use all four.
Padding makes a batch rectangular. In PyTorch, a new Embedding with padding_idx starts with a zero padding row and suppresses its lookup gradient. This option does not install attention or loss masks. A zero vector can still receive attention weight because its score participates in the softmax denominator.
shapes and flow
see also: Croft (2023)
For a batch of B=5 sequences padded to T=128 positions, lookup produces X\in\mathbb{R}^{5\times128\times d}. Transformer blocks preserve that width. Let H denote their final hidden states, including any final normalization. A separate vocabulary projection produces logits:
W_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m},\qquad
L=HW_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times m}.

shapes and flow
see also: Croft (2023)
For a batch of B=5 sequences padded to T=128 positions, lookup produces X\in\mathbb{R}^{5\times128\times d}. Transformer blocks preserve that width. Let H denote their final hidden states, including any final normalization. A separate vocabulary projection produces logits:
W_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m},\qquad
L=HW_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times m}.
An output bias may be added. Softmax runs over the vocabulary axis. With tied weights, W_{\mathrm{out}}=E^\top. Normalization and embedding scaling belong to the chosen architecture; the shape contract alone specifies neither. The original Transformer separates its decoder states from this linear projection and softmax (Vaswani et al., 2023).

  C --> D["Position-aware transformer blocks"]

masks
A causal mask prevents a position from reading future tokens. A padding mask prevents it from reading padded keys. For one batch item and attention head, an additive mask can express both:
M_{ij}=\begin{cases}
0, & j\leq i\text{ and position }j\text{ is a valid key},\\
-\infty, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\qquad
\operatorname{Attn}(Q,K,V)=
\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\right)V.
Here d_k is the query/key width. Each valid query needs at least one allowed key for this formula to be defined. Masking padded keys does not remove padded query slots or exclude their predictions from the loss. Boolean mask conventions also depend on the API: PyTorch’s scaled dot-product attention uses True for an allowed entry.
For next-token training, the logits at position t predict u_{b,t+1}. With \mathcal{M} the set of valid input–next-target pairs, the unweighted mean loss is
\mathcal{L}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|}
\sum_{(b,t)\in\mathcal{M}}
\log\operatorname{softmax}(L_{b,t,:})_{u_{b,t+1}},
\qquad |\mathcal{M}|>0.
For BOS a b EOS PAD, the supervised pairs are BOS predicting a, a predicting b, and b predicting EOS. The prediction whose target is PAD is ignored. This shift is applied once, either by preparing the targets or by the model’s loss implementation. PyTorch’s cross-entropy loss accepts logits directly and supports ignored target indices; it does not perform the sequence shift itself.
A literal [MASK] token serves another purpose. BERT uses it to hide selected input content during masked-language-model training [@devlin2019bertpretrainingdeepbidirectional]. An attention mask controls which positions can exchange information.
