Ethics (1677)
Deus sive Natura: God, or Nature (Part IV, preface). The Amsterdam Jewish community expelled Spinoza in 1656, and many readers called him an atheist. The Ethics still talks about God on almost every page. The question is what he means by the word.
God of the Philosophers/Metaphysicians

Aristotle’s unmoved mover (Metaphysics XII). Xenophanes had already described one god who does not move and who thinks.
A god reached by argument, valued by philosophers for explaining the world. It is a different god from the one ordinary believers pray to.
No personal attachments: Spinoza’s God loves and hates no one (5P17 corollary).

Monotheism: God \neq nature. God creates nature and stays outside it.
Spinoza: God = nature. God is the most powerful and perfect being, and nature is that being.
Substance
Aristotle: a substance is neither said of a subject nor exists in a subject (Categories 5, 2a11). This horse is a substance; its color exists in the horse.
Descartes: strictly only God is a substance, but created things divide into two kinds of substance, mind and body (Principles I.51–53). This is his dualism.
Parmenides: one should say and think only that Being is (fragment B6). Being is single and numerically one.
Spinoza: substance is “what is in itself and is conceived through itself” (1D3). Combine this with Parmenides’s conclusion and there can be only one substance.
What is it like? One infinite being that is alive, intelligent and all-powerful, and that is also material and spatial.

God is not a transcendent, supernatural cause. God is nature. God is the immanent cause of all things (1P18).

Self-caused
A cause of itself (causa sui) is that whose essence involves existence (1D1). Its nature cannot be conceived except as existing.
Substance cannot be produced by anything else (1P6 corollary). Nothing outside it causes it, so its existence must come from its own nature (1P7). It has to exist.
Monism

Substance is unique. There exists only one substance. Not one kind of substance, but numerically one single substance

The lecture’s version, from the principle of sufficient reason:

Self-caused
A cause of itself (causa sui) is that whose essence involves existence (1D1). Its nature cannot be conceived except as existing.
Substance cannot be produced by anything else (1P6 corollary). Nothing outside it causes it, so its existence must come from its own nature (1P7). It has to exist.
Monism

Substance is unique. There exists only one substance. Not one kind of substance, but numerically one single substance

The lecture’s version, from the principle of sufficient reason:

Something exists.
Whatever exists has a sufficient cause.
Therefore a self-caused substance must exist.
There is at most one.

Why at most one?

Two self-caused substances would have to differ in something.
A difference needs a cause.
One self-caused substance cannot cause anything in another, since each is conceived through itself (1P6). Nothing could ground the difference.

Spinoza’s own route in Part I:

Two substances cannot share an attribute (1P5).
God has all attributes (1D6).
So any second substance would share an attribute with God. There is no substance except God (1P14).

Aristotle and Spinoza on substance
For Aristotle the color exists in the horse, and the horse exists in nothing else. The horse is a primary substance. For Spinoza the horse is itself “in another”: it is a mode of God.

Nature is not a totality of things

Nature is not a totality of things

Finite things are modifications of one substance. Nature is the substance they modify, and the finite things are not parts added together to make it.
Mode and Attribute
Attribute: “that which the intellect perceives of a substance as constituting its essence” (1D4).
Substance has infinitely many attributes, and each attribute has infinitely many modes.
Mode: “the affections of a substance, or that which is in another through which it is also conceived” (1D5).
Finite modes are connected: each is caused by other finite modes, without end (1P28).
“Mode” = modification, a way of being. A mode of substance is some way in which substance is modified.
“Conceived through” = explained by, made intelligible by.
Spinoza’s idea of Substance (= God)
One single, infinite, eternal substance, comprising infinitely many attributes, each expressed in infinitely many modes.
Substance > Attribute > Mode
Divisibility implies corruption. If substance could be divided, its parts would either keep its nature, so there would be several substances, or lose it, so substance could stop existing (1P12, 1P13).
God can’t have parts and pieces. Is God divisible? No: an absolutely infinite substance is indivisible (1P13). Bodies look divisible only when we picture them in the imagination (1P15 scholium).
Definition 6: “By God I mean a being absolutely infinite, that is, a substance consisting of infinite attributes, each of which expresses eternal and infinite essence.”
Proposition 11: “God, or a substance consisting of infinite attributes, each of which expresses eternal and infinite essence, necessarily exists.”
Method for the proof of god
Ontological proof: God is a being that cannot fail to exist, because God’s essence includes existence.
Cosmological proof: God is the first cause of everything else. Without God the chain of cause and effect would go back forever, and the world would have no rational foundation. Aristotle’s proof of the unmoved mover in the Metaphysics has this form.
Teleological proof (“design argument”): nature shows evidence of intelligent design. Spinoza rejects it. Explaining nature by purposes projects human wants onto God (Part I, appendix). None of his three demonstrations of Proposition 11 uses it.
Reduction to absurdity (reductio ad absurdum)

To prove P:
  assume NP
  show that if NP, then Q & NQ
  Q and NQ is contradiction and is impossible (contradiction=False)
  so not NP
  therefore P
First proof (ontological):

Suppose God does not exist.
Axiom 7: if a thing can be conceived as not existing, its essence does not involve existence.
Proposition 7: existence belongs to the nature of substance. Why?
a. Substance cannot be produced by another.
b. So, by Definition 1, substance is self-caused, and its essence involves existence.
God is a substance, so the supposed non-existence of God contradicts Proposition 7.
Therefore, God exists.

Second proof (cosmological):

For everything there must be a cause, either of its existence or of its nonexistence.
The cause, whether of existence or non-existence, is either in the thing or in another.
A thing necessarily exists if no cause prevents its existence.
God’s nature does not contain a contradiction, so if God does not exist, the cause of non-existence must be in another thing.
What prevents God from existing would have to be another substance with nothing in common with God.
If two things have nothing in common, one cannot cause anything in the other (1P3).
Therefore, no cause prevents God’s existence.
So, God exists.

Third proof (from power):

Being able to not exist is a lack of power; being able to exist is power.
Suppose only finite things necessarily exist. Then finite things would be more powerful than an absolutely infinite being, which is absurd.
We exist, either in ourselves or in something else that necessarily exists.
So an absolutely infinite being necessarily exists.


There is nothing of which we can be more certain than the existence of an absolutely infinite or perfect being, that is, God. (1P11 scholium)

Strassen’s algorithm multiplies two square matrices with seven recursive block products instead of eight. This changes the asymptotic cost from \Theta(n^3) to \Theta(n^{\log_2 7}), where \log_2 7\approx 2.8074.
The reduction in multiplications requires more additions and subtractions. On floating-point inputs, those operations can amplify rounding error relative to classical GEMM. Practical implementations use a few Strassen levels, then switch to a tuned GEMM kernel.
history
Volker Strassen published the algorithm in 1969 in Gaussian Elimination is not Optimal. The construction proved that matrix multiplication can beat cubic arithmetic asymptotically.
algorithm
Let A and B be two square matrices over a ring \mathcal{R}. The goal is to calculate C = AB.
The algorithm partitions A, B, and C into equally sized block matrices:
A = \begin{bmatrix}A_{11}&A_{12}\\A_{21}&A_{22}\end{bmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{bmatrix}B_{11}&B_{12}\\B_{21}&B_{22}\end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{bmatrix}C_{11}&C_{12}\\C_{21}&C_{22}\end{bmatrix}
The classical block algorithm requires eight multiplications:
\begin{bmatrix}C_{11}&C_{12}\\C_{21}&C_{22}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}A_{11}B_{11}+A_{12}B_{21} & A_{11}B_{12}+A_{12}B_{22}\\A_{21}B_{11}+A_{22}B_{21} & A_{21}B_{12}+A_{22}B_{22}\end{bmatrix}
Strassen’s algorithm instead defines 7 products:
\begin{aligned}
M_1 &= (A_{11}+A_{22})(B_{11}+B_{22})\\
M_2 &= (A_{21}+A_{22})B_{11}\\
M_3 &= A_{11}(B_{12}-B_{22})\\

Strassen’s algorithm instead defines 7 products:
\begin{aligned}
M_1 &= (A_{11}+A_{22})(B_{11}+B_{22})\\
M_2 &= (A_{21}+A_{22})B_{11}\\
M_3 &= A_{11}(B_{12}-B_{22})\\
M_4 &= A_{22}(B_{21}-B_{11})\\
M_5 &= (A_{11}+A_{12})B_{22}\\
M_6 &= (A_{21}-A_{11})(B_{11}+B_{12})\\
M_7 &= (A_{12}-A_{22})(B_{21}+B_{22})
\end{aligned}
The result blocks are computed as:
\begin{bmatrix}C_{11}&C_{12}\\C_{21}&C_{22}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}M_1+M_4-M_5+M_7 & M_3+M_5\\M_2+M_4 & M_1-M_2+M_3+M_6\end{bmatrix}
The same step is applied recursively. A real implementation stops earlier and hands each small product to GEMM.
improvements
The original step uses seven multiplications and 18 additions or subtractions. Winograd’s 1971 variant keeps seven multiplications and reduces the additions to 15. Later 2008.03759⁠ (Beniamini et al., 2020)  reach 12 additions, with extra work to convert between bases. Full runtime also depends on packing, memory traffic, and basis conversion.
asymptotic complexity
For an n\times n matrix with even block sizes, the recurrence is
T(n)=7T\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+18\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)^2.
The master theorem gives
T(n)=\Theta\left(n^{\log_2 7}\right).

asymptotic complexity
For an n\times n matrix with even block sizes, the recurrence is
T(n)=7T\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+18\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)^2.
The master theorem gives
T(n)=\Theta\left(n^{\log_2 7}\right).
rank or bilinear complexity
The rank of a bilinear map \phi:\mathbf A\times\mathbf B\to\mathbf C over a field \mathbf F is
R(\phi/\mathbf F)=\min\left\{r:\begin{array}{l}
\exists f_i\in\mathbf A^*,\ g_i\in\mathbf B^*,\ w_i\in\mathbf C\\
\forall a\in\mathbf A,\ \forall b\in\mathbf B,\quad
\phi(a,b)=\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^r f_i(a)g_i(b)w_i
\end{array}\right\}.
The seven products give an upper bound of 7 for the rank of 2\times2 matrix multiplication.
cache behavior
Under the no-recomputation model, a communication-optimal Strassen schedule moves
\Theta\left(n^2+\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt M}\right)^{\log_2 7}M\right)
words between slow memory and a fast memory holding M words. For cache lines of b words, divide the transfer term by b. The exponent on M is 1-\tfrac{1}{2}\log_2 7\approx -0.4037, so the classical 1/\sqrt M denominator is wrong for Strassen. See 1109.1693⁠ (Ballard et al., 2011) .
implementation considerations

Switch to conventional GEMM below an implementation-specific crossover.
Textbook recursion is simplest for powers of two. Implementations handle odd dimensions through peeling, overlapping blocks, or a GEMM fallback.
Rectangular products need a partition for which the seven-product step saves enough multiplication to repay packing and addition costs.
A 1605.01078⁠ (Huang et al., 2016)  reported crossovers near 500\times500 for one double-precision x86 setup. Other kernels and machines can move that threshold.

Language existed before we learned to speak it. We can follow its rules without being able to explain them. Lévi-Strauss takes that possibility into anthropology: people may participate in a kinship system without knowing the rules an anthropologist uses to describe it.
The unit of explanation is a relation within a system. Calling someone an uncle tells us little about the obligations between that person and a nephew. We need the other relationships, the prescribed conduct, and the cases where conduct departs from the kinship vocabulary. In Structural Anthropology, chapter II, Lévi-Strauss distinguishes the terms for relatives from the attitudes and duties associated with them.1
what a structural explanation has to explain
A structural model specifies how its elements depend on one another and how those relations change under a transformation. Lévi-Strauss distinguishes this model from the observed social relations used to construct it. Giving a custom a place in a diagram still leaves the explanation to be tested.1
His Oedipus example makes the method easier to inspect. He groups episodes by relations: Oedipus marrying his mother and Antigone burying her brother enter a group he reads as excessive attachment to blood relations; killing a father or brother enters the opposing group. This is part of his proposed analysis, with an explicitly provisional arrangement of the evidence.2
Lévi-Strauss treats Freud‘s reading of Oedipus as another variant of the myth. His comparison includes modern psychoanalytic retellings alongside the ancient versions.2
The difficult step is choosing the relations. A persuasive reading has to account for the variants it encounters and explain why its grouping is warranted. A claimed universal structure of thought needs evidence across cases. The existence of shared rules alone leaves that claim open.
These notes began with Michael Sugrue’s lecture.

A tensor field assigns a tensor to each point of a manifold. The tensor at a point acts on vectors and covectors belonging to that point. Smoothness specifies how these assignments vary across the manifold.
For a smooth manifold M, its tangent space T_xM contains the possible velocities of curves through x. These spaces form the tangent bundle TM. Their dual spaces form the cotangent bundle T^*M.

Definition 1. 

A smooth tensor field of type (p,q) is a smooth section
T \in \Gamma\!\left((TM)^{\otimes p}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes q}\right).
Thus T(x) belongs to (T_xM)^{\otimes p}\otimes(T_x^*M)^{\otimes q}. A section chooses one element of each fiber: if \pi is the bundle projection, then \pi\circ T=\operatorname{id}_M.

A scalar field has type (0,0), a vector field has type (1,0), and a one-form has type (0,1). A metric has type (0,2) because it takes two tangent vectors and returns a number. The same tensor-product construction works for a general vector bundle E, with E in place of TM. Gualtieri, vector bundles and differential forms.
via coordinate transitions
In coordinates x^1,\ldots,x^n, write a vector field and a one-form as
X=X^i\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i},\qquad \alpha=\alpha_i\,dx^i.
Repeated upper and lower indices are summed. Under a change to coordinates y^a, the chain rule gives
\widetilde X^a=\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}X^i,
\qquad
\widetilde\alpha_a=\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^a}\alpha_i.
Each upper tensor index receives the first kind of factor; each lower index receives the second. The factors cancel when a covector acts on a vector, so \alpha_iX^i=\widetilde\alpha_a\widetilde X^a. Coordinate descriptions must agree this way on overlaps to define one field. Choquet-Bruhat, §§I.2–I.3.
For example, on the plane the radial field is
X=x\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+y\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
 =r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}.
Here x=r\cos\theta and y=r\sin\theta, on a polar coordinate patch with r>0. Its Cartesian components are (x,y); its polar components are (r,0). Applied to f=x^2+y^2=r^2, both expressions give X(f)=2r^2.
See also (McConnell, 2014; Schouten, 1951).

appendix
tensor product
For vector spaces V and W over a field \mathbb F, the tensor product V\otimes W carries a bilinear map (v,w)\mapsto v\otimes w. Its defining property is that every bilinear map b:V\times W\to Z factors through a unique linear map
\widetilde b:V\otimes W\to Z,
\qquad \widetilde b(v\otimes w)=b(v,w).
General tensors are finite sums of such products. With bases \{e_i\} and \{f_j\}, the elements e_i\otimes f_j form a basis, giving \dim(V\otimes W)=\dim V\,\dim W in finite dimensions. Conrad, tensor products and bases.
metric tensors
At each point x of an n-dimensional smooth manifold M, the tangent space T_xM is an n-dimensional vector space. A metric tensor is a smooth field of symmetric, nondegenerate bilinear forms
g_x:T_xM\times T_xM\to\mathbb R.
Symmetry means g_x(u,v)=g_x(v,u); bilinearity means linearity in each argument. Nondegeneracy means
\bigl[g_x(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\in T_xM\bigr]\implies u=0.
In coordinates, g=g_{ij}\,dx^i\otimes dx^j, where (g_{ij}) is symmetric and invertible. A Riemannian metric is positive definite, so g_x(u,u)>0 whenever u\ne0. A pseudo-Riemannian metric permits other signatures, counting the positive and negative directions of the form; its signature is constant on each connected component. Meinrenken, §12.
A Lorentzian metric has one negative direction and n-1 positive directions, or the reverse sign convention. For example, Minkowski space has
g=-dt\otimes dt+dx\otimes dx+dy\otimes dy+dz\otimes dz.

g=-dt\otimes dt+dx\otimes dx+dy\otimes dy+dz\otimes dz.
The nonzero vector u=\partial_t+\partial_x satisfies g(u,u)=0. It is null and pairs nontrivially with \partial_t, since g(u,\partial_t)=-1. The metric is nondegenerate because its matrix has determinant -1. Choquet-Bruhat, §I.5.
vector bundle
A real vector bundle consists of a base space X, a total space E, and a continuous projection \pi:E\to X. Each fiber E_x=\pi^{-1}(\{x\}) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.

compatibility condition 

Each point has an open neighborhood U\subseteq X and a homeomorphism
\varphi:U\times\mathbb R^k\longrightarrow\pi^{-1}(U)
such that \pi(\varphi(x,v))=x and v\mapsto\varphi(x,v) is a linear isomorphism onto E_x.


For a smooth vector bundle, the base and total space are smooth manifolds and the local trivializations are diffeomorphisms. On overlaps, changes of fiber coordinates have the form v\mapsto A(x)v with A(x) an invertible matrix depending smoothly on x. Kapovitch, vector bundles.

The Möbius strip illustrates a bundle over a circle. For the Möbius line bundle, extend each cross-section to an entire real line: gluing the ends reverses its coordinate, (0,v)\sim(1,-v). The bounded strip shown in the video has interval fibers. Hatcher, §1.1.
properties

The pair (U,\varphi) is a local trivialization.1
The dimension of E_x is locally constant, hence constant on each connected component of X.
If this dimension is k throughout X, the bundle has rank k.
The trivial bundle is X\times\mathbb R^k\to X, with projection (x,v)\mapsto x.

dual
The dual bundle E^*\to X has fiber
E_x^*=\operatorname{Hom}(E_x,\mathbb R).
Thus an element of a dual fiber is a linear function on the corresponding original fiber. Fiberwise evaluation pairs E^* with E. Equivalently, E^* is the Hom bundle whose fiber over x is \operatorname{Hom}(E_x,\mathbb R); this is the bundle of fiberwise linear maps from E into the trivial line bundle X\times\mathbb R.
fiber
The fiber over x is the preimage \pi^{-1}(\{x\}). A fiber bundle is the whole structure (E,B,\pi,F): total space E, base space B, continuous surjection \pi:E\to B, and typical fiber F.
Local triviality requires an open neighborhood U of every base point and a homeomorphism \varphi:\pi^{-1}(U)\to U\times F satisfying \operatorname{proj}_1\circ\varphi=\pi.2

Each pair (U,\varphi) is one local trivialization. A collection covering B is a bundle atlas. Every fiber is homeomorphic to F.3 One often writes the bundle as

bundle map
For bundles \pi_E:E\to M and \pi_F:F\to N, a bundle map consists of continuous maps \varphi:E\to F and f:M\to N satisfying
\pi_F\circ\varphi=f\circ\pi_E.

The architectural bet is simple:

Move tensors as tiles.
Keep tile queues in explicit local SRAM.
Split compute from data movement.
Scale the same fabric across a card, a box, and a rack.

Blackhole is a 120 Tensix core part in current docs. It also has 16 SiFive x280 big RISC-V cores and 180 MB of on-chip SRAM. Wormhole has 80 Tensix cores at chip level, with fewer active cores exposed by n150 and n300 board products.
The easiest arithmetic trap is the Blackhole p150 fabric number:
4 \cdot 800\ \mathrm{Gb/s}
  = 3200\ \mathrm{Gb/s}
  = 400\ \mathrm{GB/s}.
The raw line rate is 400 GB/s before protocol overhead, topology, collective algorithms, and congestion. Writing this as 3.2 TB/s is a bits-to-bytes bug.
The NVIDIA H100 SXM row is useful as a scale marker because NVIDIA publishes both HBM bandwidth and NVLink bandwidth in one table. That table lists 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth and 900 GB/s NVLink bandwidth for the 80 GB SXM part. (NVIDIA, 2026)
\frac{900\ \mathrm{GB/s}}{400\ \mathrm{GB/s}} = 2.25.
So a p150 card’s four-port external fabric has about 1/2.25 of an H100 SXM NVLink aggregate budget at raw line rate. The two fabrics use different topologies. The ratio establishes one narrow point: fabric math becomes a first-order constraint once collectives dominate.
the useful atom
The useful atom is one Tensix core running compute kernels and data-movement kernels that talk through circular buffers.
The local picture is:

A reader kernel pulls tiles from DRAM or another core.
It pushes those tiles into a circular buffer in local SRAM.
A compute kernel pops tiles, runs the tile operation, and pushes output tiles.
A writer kernel drains output tiles back to DRAM or onward through the fabric.

It pushes those tiles into a circular buffer in local SRAM.
A compute kernel pops tiles, runs the tile operation, and pushes output tiles.
A writer kernel drains output tiles back to DRAM or onward through the fabric.

This is why Tenstorrent feels closer to a dataflow machine than to a CUDA block with a large invisible runtime behind it. CUDA lets a lot of people defer locality decisions to libraries. TT-Metalium makes locality part of the program text.
A circular buffer in TT-Metalium is a bounded queue with one producer and one consumer. The important API fact is that cb_reserve_back blocks until the requested pages are free. (Tenstorrent, 2026b)
That changes the failure model. A bad program can starve, deadlock, or feed tiles in the wrong order. Treat the buffer as a synchronized queue rather than a C ring buffer that silently overwrites unread tiles.
The performance question for a kernel is mechanical:
T_{\mathrm{step}}
  =
  \max\left(
    T_{\mathrm{read}},
    T_{\mathrm{compute}},
    T_{\mathrm{write}}
  \right)
  + T_{\mathrm{sync}}.
If the pipeline is healthy, reads, compute, and writes overlap. If one stage stalls, all stages inherit the slowest stage. This is the whole game. Keep the queues fed, keep the tile order correct, keep synchronization out of the inner loop.
what the software stack is now
The stack has four public layers worth naming.

TT-Metalium is the low-level C++ programming model for kernels, buffers, command queues, and devices. (Tenstorrent, 2024c, 2024b)
TT-NN is the Python and C++ neural-network op layer on top of TT-Metalium. Current docs describe more than 200 operations, mesh devices, custom ops, graph tracing, parameter caching, and comparison mode. (Tenstorrent, 2026c)
TT-MLIR is the compiler infrastructure. Public docs name TTIR as the frontend dialect and TTNN or TTMetal as backend paths, with flatbuffer serialization and runtime support. (Tenstorrent, 2024d, 2026c)
TT-XLA packages a PJRT plugin with thin JAX and PyTorch/XLA wrappers. It feeds StableHLO into the Tenstorrent compiler path. (Tenstorrent, 2026e)

The current question is coverage and maturity. A model is easy when it already has a TT-NN lowering, a TT-Metal demo, or a TT-XLA path with the needed ops. A model gets expensive when it falls through to custom kernels, strange layouts, or collectives that the compiler cannot yet make boring.

Tenstorrent has a clean shot when the workload has these properties:

That describes a lot of inference. It also describes training kernels after enough compiler work. The bet gets worse as soon as the workload needs fine-grained synchronization, irregular indexing, dynamic shapes, or frequent all-reduce across a large topology.
The hardware wants a program shaped like this:
\text{tiles in}
  \rightarrow
\text{local SRAM queues}
  \rightarrow
\text{Tensix compute}
  \rightarrow
\text{tiles out}.
The compiler has to keep that shape intact across the whole graph. Once the graph falls back to the host, or inserts extra layout conversions, the machine starts paying for its own explicitness.
the real comparison to GPUs
The honest comparison is ecosystem depth per watt-dollar, with kernel coverage as the hidden multiplier.
For a mature CUDA path, the working set is:
\text{model}
  \rightarrow
\text{PyTorch}
  \rightarrow
\text{cuDNN or CUTLASS or custom CUDA}
  \rightarrow
\text{GPU}.
For Tenstorrent, the working set is:
\text{model}
  \rightarrow
\text{TT-NN, TT-XLA, or TT-Forge}
  \rightarrow
\text{TT-MLIR}
  \rightarrow
\text{TT-Metalium}
  \rightarrow
\text{Tensix}.
That extra visibility is powerful when the path is optimized. It is painful when a needed op has no mature lowering. Useful due diligence starts with the exact model, sequence length, batch shape, precision, collective pattern, and runtime release. Peak FLOPS alone cannot answer that query.
scratch rules
When checking a Tenstorrent claim, use this order:

a game theory thought experiment involves two rational agents, each of whom can cooperate for mutual benefit or “defect” for individual reward.

In spring 1967, Ron Jones organised the Third Wave at Cubberley High School in Palo Alto to teach students about fascism. The school newspaper describes it in three sophomore Contemporary World classes and places its final rally on Wednesday, April 5. Klink (1967)
The familiar five-day story comes from Jones’s later account, which follows a Monday-to-Friday sequence. The participant-run archive records disagreement about the duration. That leaves the often-repeated April 3–7 dates unsupported by the contemporary report.
the exercise in Jones’s account
Jones began with posture drills and rules for answering questions. Students stood to speak, addressed him formally, and practised following commands quickly. He added slogans about discipline, community, and action, together with a raised, curved-hand salute. Membership cards made the group explicit. Students recruited classmates and reported breaches of the rules; Jones recalled receiving reports from more students than he had assigned to the task.
He then claimed that their classroom belonged to a national movement and called a rally to hear its leader. The promised television announcement never arrived. Jones disclosed the deception and showed film material about Nazi Germany. This sequence is the teacher’s retrospective narration, first published nationally in 1976 as Take As Directed. Jones (1976)
what the account supports
The contemporary report documents organised obedience and a staged political movement. TheWaveHome’s participant summary also records resistance, students who thought they were playing a game, and students who believed Jones’s claims.
These accounts supply no control group or independent measure of political belief. Jones introduced rules, rewards, symbols, and peer reporting together, while retaining his authority as a teacher. The episode cannot isolate the effect of a salute or establish a rate at which people become fascists. A student’s compliance could reflect belief, trust in the teacher, enjoyment of the activity, or fear of standing out.
Jones later said he would not repeat the exercise because it had put children in danger. Lipsett (2008)
aftermath
Jones was denied tenure two years later. The participant archive disputes the familiar story that the Third Wave caused his departure, so that causal claim needs separate evidence.

bostrom’s vulnerable world hypothesis is a conditional model, not a prophecy. Continued technological development may produce a capability that makes civilizational devastation very likely while humanity remains in what he calls the “semi-anarchic default condition.” The paper leaves both claims open: the black ball may never exist, and past technology has mostly helped humanity.
the “semi-anarchic default condition” names the world order we already have. States cannot prevent almost every action that nearly everyone condemns. States also lack a reliable way to solve coordination problems when national security interests conflict. Human motives remain diverse enough that a small “apocalyptic residual” may try to cause mass harm.
the model
Bostrom asks us to treat invention as drawing balls from an urn. White balls help, grey balls have mixed effects, and a black ball would create a civilizational vulnerability. Once the relevant knowledge has spread, people cannot reliably remove it from the world.
The urn is a model of the policy problem. It does not imply that discoveries arrive in a random order or that every possible technology will be built. Some capabilities depend on earlier discoveries, tacit knowledge, capital, and institutions. Bostrom discusses this through linked and textured balls. Protective technology may also change what a later discovery does.
The paper defines civilizational devastation as at least 15\% of the world population dying, or world output falling by more than 50\% for at least a decade. Those thresholds are stipulations. They keep the argument fixed to a scale of harm instead of letting “catastrophe” expand sentence by sentence.
four kinds of vulnerability



Type
Mechanism
Paper’s counterfactual




Type 1
An individual or small group can cause devastation with common materials and modest skill.
Nuclear weapons are as easy to make as a battery.


Type 2a
Great powers have strong incentives to take actions that can destroy civilization.
Nuclear weapons allow a safe first strike and no secure retaliation.


Type 2b
Many ordinary, individually useful actions add up to devastation.
Fossil fuel use causes far more warming than it does in our world.


Type 0
A project that appears acceptable contains a hidden catastrophic effect.
A physics experiment can destroy the world because its risk was miscalculated.

Type 2b

Type 0
A project that appears acceptable contains a hidden catastrophic effect.
A physics experiment can destroy the world because its risk was miscalculated.



The types separate motive from access. Type 1 depends on broad access and a small destructive minority. Type 2a can occur among leaders who prefer peace because the strategic incentives reward attack. Type 2b needs no single destructive actor. Type 0 can occur even when every actor would stop after learning the true risk.
stabilization
Bostrom groups possible responses under four headings. General relinquishment stops technological development across a wide area. Differential development speeds up protective technology while delaying dangerous technology. Restricted access keeps dangerous capabilities away from most actors. Preference modification changes the motives that produce destructive action.
Partial measures can reduce risk without making the world stable under the definition in the paper. Full stabilization requires closing the governance gap that matches the vulnerability:

The micro gap concerns actions by individuals and small groups. Type 1 may require preventive policing that catches almost every prohibited attempt.
The macro gap concerns coordination among states. Type 2 vulnerabilities may require global rules that remain effective when a state expects a large advantage from defecting.

The paper’s “freedom tag” is a thought experiment for the micro gap. Each person would wear cameras and microphones, encrypted recordings would be sent for automated review, and suspicious activity would reach a human analyst. Bostrom estimates about 140 per person each year, or less than 1\% of world output. He also names the obvious failure mode. The same system could support permanent tyranny. Privacy rules, access controls, and public oversight therefore belong inside the stabilization problem.
Effective global governance in this model means capacity, not democratic legitimacy. A hegemonic state could satisfy the narrow condition if it could impose and enforce a solution. That creates a second problem. A system with enough power to prevent catastrophic coordination failures may also have enough power to lock in bad rules. Legitimacy affects compliance, resistance, and the number of people willing to attack the system. It cannot be added after the capacity question is solved.
AI and the framework
AI is not an established black ball. The framework becomes useful only after a claim specifies the dangerous capability, who can access it, what motivates use, and which institution fails to contain it.
One capability can also occupy more than one type. A system that lowers the skill needed for biological design could widen access and create a Type 1 risk. Competition among states or firms could create Type 2a incentives before that access becomes broad. An unexpected autonomous failure would instead resemble Type 0. Each mechanism requires different evidence and a different response.
Model diffing can identify a behavioral change between models. It does not prevent deployment, restrict access, or solve coordination, so it is a diagnostic tool rather than a stabilization mechanism. AI may also lower the cost of monitoring and analysis. That makes both dangerous capabilities and intrusive governance cheaper.
where the model is weak
The paper gives a clear classification and a thin account of political change. Motives are treated as a stable distribution even though institutions can change them. Governance capacity is separated from legitimacy even though legitimacy changes the cost of enforcement. The analysis also has little historical reference data for estimating how often a discovery produces the stipulated scale of harm.
These limits do not make probabilities over new risks meaningless. They make them sensitive to the reference class and model assumptions. The useful output is a range tied to explicit mechanisms, followed by a decision that can survive large error bars.
the remaining questions are practical:

Which current capabilities are becoming easier to access faster than defenses are improving?
Which institutions could close a governance gap without creating another failure mode?

A language model receives token IDs. Text reaches the tokenizer after decoding into Unicode or as raw bytes. UTF-8 writes Unicode scalar values as bytes. The tokenizer groups text or bytes into vocabulary pieces and maps each piece to an integer.
ascii
ASCII assigns 128 values, so each value fits in seven bits. Values 0 to 31 are control characters, and value 127 is DEL. Values 32 to 126 are the 95 printable characters, including space. An eight-bit representation of an ASCII value has a leading zero; ASCII does not define an eighth bit.
In ASCII, each Latin uppercase and lowercase pair differs by bit 0x20. Python makes the representation visible:

format(ord('Y'), '07b')  # '1011001'
format(ord('y'), '07b')  # '1111001'
“Extended ASCII” does not name one standard. It refers to several incompatible eight-bit encodings that reused values 128 to 255.
unicode and utf-8
Unicode defines a code space from U+0000 through U+10FFFF. A Unicode scalar value is any code point in that range outside the surrogate range U+D800 through U+DFFF. Unicode assigns abstract characters to code points inside the code space. A code point is still not the same thing as a visible character. One grapheme can contain several code points.
UTF-8 encodes each Unicode scalar value as one to four bytes. ASCII values keep their one-byte representation. Other values use a leading byte followed by continuation bytes.

'😋'.encode('utf-8')  # b'\xf0\x9f\x98\x8b'
model tokens
The model and tokenizer share one fixed vocabulary. Changing the tokenizer changes the token IDs and therefore changes which embedding row the model reads.
A pure byte tokenizer can represent any UTF-8 byte stream with 256 base values, though long common strings then occupy many tokens. Byte-level BPE starts from those byte values and learns merges, keeping byte coverage while shortening frequent byte sequences. A whole-word vocabulary gives frequent words short sequences, though names, spelling variants, and new words either enlarge the vocabulary or require an unknown token. Subword tokenizers learn pieces between those two extremes. Frequent strings may stay whole, while rarer strings split into smaller pieces.
The exact split depends on the learned vocabulary and its boundary rules. annoyingly might be one token, several meaningful-looking pieces, or a sequence that cuts across morphemes. Token boundaries follow the learned vocabulary, so they need not match morphemes.
subword methods
byte-pair encoding
Subword BPE learns an ordered list of frequent pair merges and applies those merges to new text (Sennrich et al., 2016). GPT-2 uses byte-level BPE with a 256-byte base vocabulary (Radford et al., 2019).
byte-pair-encoding 
wordpiece
Original BERT uses a 30,000-token WordPiece vocabulary (Devlin et al., 2019). Its released tokenizer applies basic text processing, then scans each word with greedy longest-match-first search. A continuation piece begins with ##, and a word becomes [UNK] when the vocabulary cannot cover the complete word. The paper specifies the vocabulary size and token format, while the released tokenizer specifies encoding.

tracing garbage collection keeps objects reachable from a root set and reclaims the rest. tri-color marking tracks the reached objects whose pointers still need scanning, and write barriers keep that state correct while the program changes pointers. Go uses precise, concurrent, non-generational, non-compacting mark-sweep. Go 1.26 made Green Tea the default marking implementation.12


reachability
Treat the heap as a directed graph. Objects are vertices and pointers are edges. Roots are references held in stacks, globals, and runtime data structures. The collector computes the transitive closure of the roots and reclaims vertices outside it.
Reachability overapproximates future use. A reachable object may never affect the program again, yet deciding that property in general would require predicting future execution. Tracing collectors therefore reclaim unreachable garbage and may retain semantic garbage.
tri-color marking
The colors describe one marking cycle:

white objects have not been reached.
gray objects have been reached, but their outgoing pointers have not all been scanned.
black objects have been reached and scanned.

The collector starts with gray roots. Scanning a gray object turns it black and shades each white successor gray. When the gray worklist is empty, every remaining white object is unreachable for that cycle.

flowchart LR
    Roots[root jobs] --> Gray[gray worklist]
    Gray --> Scan[scan pointers]
    Scan --> Black[black object]
    Scan -->|shade white successor| Gray
    Barrier[pointer write barrier] --> Gray
    Black --> Done{gray worklist empty}
    Done --> Sweep[sweep white objects]

An incremental collector must prevent the mutator from hiding a white object behind an already scanned black object. Write barriers record the relevant pointer changes. Go’s current hybrid barrier shades both the overwritten pointer and the new pointer value during marking.1
collector families
Mark-sweep traces the live graph, then walks allocation units and returns unmarked storage to free lists. Marking costs O(V_{\mathrm{live}}+E_{\mathrm{live}}) for the reachable graph. Sweeping costs O(H) over the heap units being swept.
Evacuating collectors move live survivors into another region and reclaim the old region at once. Mark-compact collectors also move live objects, then leave free memory contiguous. Generation and region are policies for choosing which part of the heap to collect. They do not determine whether survivors move.
Go’s collector
The runtime describes Go’s collector as precise, parallel, concurrent mark-sweep with a write barrier. It is non-generational and non-compacting.1 A cycle has two short global stops. The first enables the barrier and prepares root jobs. Mark workers and allocation assists scan roots and gray objects while the program runs. The second stop ends marking. Sweeping then proceeds concurrently and on demand during allocation.
Go 1.25 introduced Green Tea as an experiment. Go 1.26 enabled it by default.2 Green Tea keeps the same reachability semantics and reorganizes marking work around spans so small objects on the same page can be scanned together. This improves locality and CPU scaling when each page contains enough live objects that need scanning. The Go team reports a 10% to 40% reduction in GC overhead for programs that spend substantial time in the collector, with results depending on heap shape.3
pacing and memory
The Go guide models one cycle’s CPU cost as a fixed cost plus work proportional to the live heap and roots:
C_{\mathrm{cycle}} \approx C_{\mathrm{fixed}} + c_{\mathrm{scan}}\left(H_{\mathrm{live}} + R_{\mathrm{roots}}\right).
GOGC controls how much new heap may accumulate before the next cycle:

Under the guide’s steady-state assumptions, doubling GOGC roughly doubles heap overhead and halves GC CPU cost. It changes the collection target, while the program determines the live set. GOMEMLIMIT adds a soft limit for runtime-managed memory. The runtime increases collection pressure near that limit, but it may exceed the limit to avoid spending more than about half of available CPU time in GC.4
Pause time needs measurement. Stack scanning, scheduler delays at safe points, mark termination, and operating-system effects can each dominate a particular workload. runtime/metrics, GODEBUG=gctrace=1, CPU profiles, and pause histograms expose different parts of that cost.
Rust
Rust uses ownership and deterministic destruction for its standard allocation model. Strong Rc<T> cycles can still leak because their reference counts never reach zero; Weak<T> breaks the usual parent-child cycle.5
Programs that need traced cyclic subgraphs can opt into a separate heap. zerogc exposes explicit safepoints through an implementation-independent API.6 gc-arena confines traced pointers to a branded arena with one root and uses incremental mark-sweep.7 These crates collect only the objects placed in their heaps. Ordinary Rust allocation still uses ownership and deterministic destruction.

properties of being that are universal to all beings

In medieval scholastic philosophy, transcendentals are concepts that apply across the categories of being. A substance can be one, and so can a quality. Unity therefore exceeds the scope of either category. Common examples are being, one, true, and good; medieval philosophers disagree about their number and how they relate. Goris and Aertsen’s account⁠ traces these differences.
For Aquinas, these terms differ in meaning while referring to the same beings. Calling something one considers its lack of division in itself. Calling it true considers its relation to an intellect, and calling it good considers it as desirable. Goodness in this metaphysical sense concerns a thing’s actuality and perfection; a separate argument is needed to establish moral goodness.
truth.
Aquinas says that truth belongs primarily to the intellect when its judgment agrees with what is. Things are called true through their relation to an intellect. His claim that being and truth are convertible means that every being is intelligible in principle. The existence of a judgment alone gives us no guarantee that its content agrees with reality. See Summa theologiae I, question 16, articles 1–3.
Kant uses transcendental for an inquiry into the a priori conditions of our cognition of objects, meaning the conditions that can be known independently of experience. This is the usage behind transcendental idealism. The scholastic doctrine concerns the common attributes of being; Kant’s inquiry concerns how cognition of objects is possible. See the introduction to the Critique of Pure Reason, A11–12/B25.

A transformer combines attention with position-wise feed-forward layers, residual connections, and normalization. Attention lets each position read weighted combinations of other positions’ value vectors. The weights come from query–key scores computed from the current representations using learned projections. A high weight says where information enters that computation; it does not identify a high-entropy token or guarantee semantic importance. (Vaswani et al., 2023)
The architecture and the training objective are separate choices. The original transformer had an encoder and a decoder for translation. Here I focus on a decoder-only autoregressive language model: read a prefix, produce a distribution for the next token, append a token, repeat. 1706.03762⁠ (Vaswani et al., 2023) . There is also a more recent blog post that goes beyond just a simple GPT-like architecture (probably a bit more updated with Kimi, Gated Delta Rule, et al.)

A transformer uses memory for weights, temporary activations, and, during cached decoding, previous keys and values. Dense attention over a sequence of length T computes T^2 query–key scores per head. Implementations can avoid storing the complete score matrix; that changes memory traffic and storage without removing all those interactions. 2009.06732⁠ (Tay et al., 2022) 
For an ordinary uncompressed KV cache with L layers, B sequences of length T, h_{\mathrm{KV}} key/value heads, equal key and value width d_h, and s bytes per element:
\operatorname{KVBytes}=2BLTh_{\mathrm{KV}}d_hs.
The factor of two counts keys and values. Under these assumptions, doubling the context doubles cache storage. temperature
For \tau>0:

The low-temperature limit is uniform over exact ties. An implementation’s greedy mode can choose one tied token through a separate tie-breaking rule.
For fixed finite logits, entropy is nondecreasing with temperature:
H(p^{(\tau)})=-\sum_i p_i^{(\tau)}\log p_i^{(\tau)},
\qquad
\frac{dH}{d\tau}=\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{p^{(\tau)}}(z)}{\tau^3}\geq0.
This follows by differentiating the softmax partition function. It concerns the next-token distribution before any truncation. It does not establish the quality or diversity of complete answers.
top-k
Choose a deterministic ordering for probability ties, and let S_k contain the first k tokens in descending probability order. Keep those tokens and renormalize:
p_i^{(k)}=\frac{p_i\mathbf1[i\in S_k]}{\sum_{j\in S_k}p_j}.
Exactly k candidates survive under this definition. A threshold implementation that keeps every token tied with the kth token can retain more. The parameter fixes a count even when probability is distributed unevenly across those candidates.
top-p (nucleus)
Write the descending probabilities as p_{(1)},\ldots,p_{(|\mathcal V|)}. For a mass threshold \rho\in(0,1], choose
k_\rho=\min\left\{k:\sum_{j=1}^{k}p_{(j)}\geq\rho\right\}.

Exactly k candidates survive under this definition. A threshold implementation that keeps every token tied with the kth token can retain more. The parameter fixes a count even when probability is distributed unevenly across those candidates.
top-p (nucleus)
Write the descending probabilities as p_{(1)},\ldots,p_{(|\mathcal V|)}. For a mass threshold \rho\in(0,1], choose
k_\rho=\min\left\{k:\sum_{j=1}^{k}p_{(j)}\geq\rho\right\}.
Retain the first k_\rho tokens, including the token that crosses the threshold, and renormalize. The number retained changes with the distribution. A direct implementation sorts the vocabulary; this is an implementation choice, not a requirement that every sampler use a full sort. (Holtzman et al., 2020) 1904.09751⁠ (Holtzman et al., 2020) 
min-p
For a relative threshold m\in[0,1], retain
S_m=\{i:p_i\geq m\max_j p_j\}.
Then renormalize on S_m. At m=0, every token survives; at m=1, only the maxima survive. For positive m after temperature scaling, the same condition can be written without computing probabilities:
z_i-z_{\max}\geq\tau\log m.
This makes the interaction with temperature explicit. Increasing \tau widens the allowed logit gap for fixed m.
Nguyen et al. report gains from min-p, including at high temperatures. (Nguyen et al., 2025) A subsequent 2506.13681⁠ (Schaeffer et al., 2025)  disputes the claimed advantage after checking the evaluations and matching hyperparameter searches. The relative probability floor defines the method; superiority over top-p remains an empirical claim to evaluate for the model, task, and tuning budget.

KV
A KV cache stores the key and value representations from earlier positions at each cached layer. In a causal model, appending a token leaves those earlier representations unchanged, so the next query can reuse them. Caching avoids recomputing the prefix; the query still has to attend over the available keys and values.
Mooncake organizes serving around this cache and prefill and decode disaggregation. Its cache transfers and placement policies are system-level choices. (Qin et al., 2024)

Ordinary autoregressive sampling draws one token from the distribution conditioned on the existing prefix:
x_{t+1}\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t}),
\qquad
p_\theta(x_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).

Gloeckle et al. train several output prediction heads on a shared trunk. Each head predicts a different future offset from the same prefix representation. These heads are distinct from the attention heads inside a transformer block. (Gloeckle et al., 2024) 2404.19737⁠ (Gloeckle et al., 2024) 
For a sequence of length T, let q_{\theta,r}(\cdot\mid x_{\leq t}) be the distribution from offset head r. One token-averaged objective is

\log q_{\theta,r}(x_{t+r}\mid x_{\leq t}),

All heads must contribute gradients to the shared trunk. Write its sequence of hidden states as h=f_{\theta_{\mathrm{trunk}}}(x), and let \ell_r be the loss from head r. The chain rule gives

Byte-Latent Transformer
2412.09871⁠ (Pagnoni et al., 2024)  models raw bytes through three stages: a local encoder groups byte representations into patches, a larger transformer processes the patch sequence, and a local decoder predicts bytes. Patch boundaries depend on a smaller model’s next-byte entropy estimates. Predictable stretches can use longer patches, reducing the number of positions processed by the large transformer.
This removes a fixed subword tokenizer. The byte representation, patching rule, and local encoder/decoder still determine how text enters and leaves the model.

Let s_0 be the initial string, M_t(s_t\mid s_{t-1}) a normalized transition kernel, and G_t(s_{t-1},s_t)\geq0 a potential. Use a fixed horizon H here to make termination explicit. An EOS-terminated string is absorbing, with a self-transition and potential one on subsequent steps. The path target is
\gamma_H(s_{1:H})=\prod_{t=1}^{H}M_t(s_t\mid s_{t-1})G_t(s_{t-1},s_t),
\qquad
\pi_H(s_{1:H})=\frac{\gamma_H(s_{1:H})}{Z_H},
\qquad
Z_H=\sum_{s_{1:H}}\gamma_H(s_{1:H}).
This requires 0<Z_H<\infty. The endpoint distribution is the marginal of \pi_H at s_H. Sequences that have not reached EOS by H remain truncated prefixes unless the target explicitly excludes them. An unbounded construction needs assumptions about termination and integrability before taking a limit.
A simple bootstrap particle approximation proceeds as follows. This is the standard with-replacement construction, separate from Lew et al.’s branching and without-replacement algorithm. Doucet and Johansen’s particle-filter tutorial

Start with N copies of s_0, each with normalized weight W_0^{(i)}=1/N.
At each t\in\{1,\ldots,H\}, draw ancestor indices A_t^{(i)}\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(W_{t-1}), then propose S_t^{(i)}\sim M_t(\cdot\mid S_{t-1}^{(A_t^{(i)})}).
Set g_t^{(i)}=G_t(S_{t-1}^{(A_t^{(i)})},S_t^{(i)}), and normalize W_t^{(i)}=g_t^{(i)}/\sum_jg_t^{(j)}.
If every weight is zero, this particle population has failed. It cannot be normalized. At the horizon, use \sum_i W_H^{(i)}\delta_{S_H^{(i)}} as the endpoint approximation.

Resampling favors prefixes that have accumulated weight. Finite populations can lose useful continuations, especially when constraints only become informative near the end. The weighted empirical measure is an approximation; its normalized probabilities are not generally unbiased.
With finite integrable potentials, the bootstrap normalizer estimate is
\widehat Z_H=\prod_{t=1}^{H}\left(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}g_t^{(i)}\right).

Under the stated multinomial resampling scheme it is unbiased for Z_H. A population that reaches zero total weight contributes \widehat Z_H=0. VC dimension measures the capacity of a binary hypothesis class. The class specifies the available classifiers; a learning algorithm chooses among them. To measure this capacity, ask whether the class can fit every possible labeling of a given finite set of points.

Definition 1. 

Represent each classifier by the subset of X that it labels positive, giving a nonempty set family H\subseteq\mathcal{P}(X). For a finite set C\subseteq X, the trace of H on C is
H|_C\coloneqq\{h\cap C:h\in H\}.
Each member of the trace is a set of points in C that some classifier labels positive. The class shatters C when every subset is available:
H|_C=\mathcal{P}(C)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\lvert H|_C\rvert=2^{|C|}.
Its VC dimension is
\operatorname{VCdim}(H)=\sup\{|C|:C\subseteq X\text{ is finite and shattered by }H\}.


If arbitrarily large finite sets can be shattered, this dimension is \infty. A finite dimension d means that some set of d points is shattered and no set of d+1 points is. Different labelings can use different classifiers. See Mohri’s lecture, slides 20–22.
For example, let H contain all closed intervals on the real line, with points inside an interval labeled positive. Given two points x_1<x_2, an interval can contain neither point, only the first, only the second, or both. All four labelings are possible.
For any three points x_1<x_2<x_3, the labeling (+1,-1,+1) is impossible: an interval containing both endpoints also contains the middle point. Thus \operatorname{VCdim}(H)=2, even though the class contains infinitely many intervals.

a mechanical device used to determine the optimal1 location of a warehouse for distributing goods to a set of shops.

The frame consists of a board with n holes corresponding to n shops at locations \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n. Strings are tied together at one end, passed through the holes, and attached to weights below the board. At equilibrium position \mathbf{v}, this point minimizes the weighted sum of distances:
D(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}\|
This optimization problem is called the Weber problem.
mechanical problem - optimization problem
At equilibrium point \mathbf{v}, the sum of all forces equals zero. For holes at locations \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n with weights m_1, \ldots, m_n, the force on the i-th string has magnitude m_i \cdot g and direction \frac{\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{v}\|}.
Canceling the common term g:
\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{v}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i \frac{\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{v}\|} = \mathbf{0}
This nonlinear system can be solved iteratively using the Weiszfeld algorithm.
The connection between equations is:
\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) =  \nabla D(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial D}{\partial x} \\ \frac{\partial D}{\partial y} \end{bmatrix}
Therefore, function D has a local extremum at point \mathbf{v}, and the Varignon frame provides the optimal location experimentally.
special cases: n=1 and n=2

For n = 1: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{x}_1
For n = 2 and m_2 > m_1: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{x}_2
For n = 2 and m_2 = m_1: \mathbf{v} can be any point on line segment \overline{X_1X_2}

For n = 1: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{x}_1

For n = 2 and m_2 = m_1: \mathbf{v} can be any point on line segment \overline{X_1X_2}

In the equal weights case, level curves are confocal ellipses with \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2 as common foci.
weiszfeld algorithm and fixed point problem
Replacing \mathbf{v} in the equilibrium equation yields the iteration:
\mathbf{v}_{k+1} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{m_i \mathbf{x}_i}{\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{v}_k\|}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{m_i}{\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{v}_k\|}}
A suitable starting point is the center of mass:
\mathbf{v}_0 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i \mathbf{x}_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i}
This can be viewed as finding the fixed point of function:
\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{m_i \mathbf{x}_i}{\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}\|}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{m_i}{\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}\|}}
with fixed point equation \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{x}).
Note: The algorithm may have numerical issues when \mathbf{v}_k is close to any point \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n.

Continuous first-order partial derivatives near \mathbf{x} are sufficient for this. The Jacobian maps an input displacement to the first-order output displacement. See MIT’s notes on derivatives of vector functions.

see also gradient descent
For a differentiable scalar function f on Euclidean space with its standard inner product, the gradient is the vector that represents the derivative through the dot product:2
Df(\mathbf{x})[\mathbf{v}]
=\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\cdot\mathbf{v},
\qquad
df=\nabla f\cdot d\mathbf{r}.
The differential gives the first-order change associated with a displacement. For a unit vector \mathbf{u}, it gives the rate of change per unit distance in that direction. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
D_{\mathbf{u}}f(\mathbf{x})
=\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\cdot\mathbf{u}
\leq\|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|,
\qquad \|\mathbf{u}\|=1.
If the gradient is nonzero, equality holds for \mathbf{u}=\nabla f/\|\nabla f\|. This is the direction of fastest first-order increase, with rate \|\nabla f\|. Fixing the direction’s length matters: allowing arbitrarily long vectors would make the rate unbounded. If \nabla f=0, every directional derivative is zero and first-order information picks no preferred direction. The point could still be a minimum, a maximum, or a saddle. See MIT’s gradient and directional derivative notes.

vector field

vector field
A vector field assigns a vector to each point of its domain. For S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, this is a map V:S\to\mathbb{R}^n. A velocity field, for instance, assigns the local velocity to each position.
On an open subset S, a smooth vector field can be written in Cartesian coordinates as
V(\mathbf{x})
=\sum_{i=1}^n V_i(\mathbf{x})
\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\right|_{\mathbf{x}}.
Here the coordinate vectors \partial/\partial x_i form the tangent-space basis at \mathbf{x}, and the smooth functions V_i give the components. In Euclidean coordinates, this is the same vector usually written (V_1(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,V_n(\mathbf{x})).

A vector space V over a field F, such as \mathbb{R} or \mathbb{C}, is a set equipped with vector addition and scalar multiplication. Both operations stay inside V:
u+v\in V, \qquad av\in V
\quad\text{for }u,v\in V,\ a\in F.
The operations must satisfy the following rules for all u,v,w\in V and a,b\in F:
\begin{aligned}
u+v &= v+u, & (u+v)+w &= u+(v+w), \\
v+0 &= v, & v+(-v) &= 0, \\
1v &= v, & a(bv) &= (ab)v, \\
a(u+v) &= au+av, & (a+b)v &= av+bv.
\end{aligned}
Here 0\in V is the additive identity, and each v has an additive inverse -v\in V. These are requirements on the operations. An arbitrary set has no addition or scalar multiplication built in. See Axler, §1B.

coordinates and subspaces
linear combination
Choose vectors g_1,\ldots,g_n\in V. A linear combination is a vector
v=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i g_i, \qquad a_i\in F.
The scalars a_i are its coefficients. Allowing every choice of coefficients gives the span of these vectors.
linear independence, span and basis
The vectors are linearly independent when
\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i g_i=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a_1=\cdots=a_n=0.
For a finite-dimensional space, an ordered basis is a linearly independent spanning list. Spanning ensures every vector in V can be represented; independence makes its coefficients unique. Those coefficients, in the chosen basis order, are the vector’s coordinates. See Treil, §1.2.
For example, B=((1,1),(1,-1)) is a basis of \mathbb{R}^2, since

(x,y)=\frac{x+y}{2}(1,1)+\frac{x-y}{2}(1,-1).
In this basis, (3,1) has coordinates (2,1). Coordinates depend on the basis we choose.
subspace
A subspace U\subseteq V contains 0 and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, using the operations of V. It inherits the other vector-space rules. See Axler, §1C.
The line \{(t,t):t\in\mathbb{R}\} is a subspace of \mathbb{R}^2. The shifted line \{(t,t+1):t\in\mathbb{R}\} fails the test because it omits (0,0).

excerpt from Nietzsche‘s Beyond Good and Evil, §1

The will to truth, which is still going to tempt us to many a hazardous enterprise; that celebrated veracity of which all philosophers have hitherto spoken with reverence: what questions this will to truth has already set before us! What strange, wicked, questionable questions! It is already a long story — yet does it not seem as if it has only just begun? Is it any wonder we should at last grow distrustful, lose our patience, turn impatiently away? That this sphinx should teach us too to ask questions? Who really is it that here questions us? What really is it in us that wants ‘the truth’?

Nietzsche asks why philosophers want truth and why they rank it above uncertainty or ignorance. A commitment to truth already contains a judgment about what is worth pursuing. What justifies that judgment? The question becomes hazardous when inquiry turns on the value that has guided it.

We did indeed pause for a long time before the question of the origin of this will — until finally we came to a complete halt before an even more fundamental question. We asked after the value of this will. Granted we want truth: why not rather untruth? And uncertainty? Even ignorance? — The problem of the value of truth stepped before us — or was it we who stepped before this problem? Which of us is Oedipus here? Which of us sphinx? It is, it seems, a rendezvous of questions and question-marks. And, would you believe it, it has finally almost come to seem to us that this problem has never before been posed — that we have been the first to see it, to fix our eye on it, to hazard it? For there is a hazard in it and perhaps there exists no greater hazard

The opening sections put that value under examination. In §4, Nietzsche asks what a judgment does for life, including when the judgment is false. This gives truth-seeking another question to answer: what does the pursuit serve?

The world is the totality of facts, not of things.Wittgenstein, Tractatus 1.1, Ogden translation
I enjoyed reading through a few of Wittgenstein’s notebooks. The two books give me a more specific question to follow: what makes a proposition meaningful, and what happens when we expect every use of language to work the same way?
“The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.” TLP 5.6, Ogden translation. 
The limit in TLP concerns what a proposition can represent. Reading it as a claim that someone’s vocabulary fixes every thought they can have imports a psychological theory. Wittgenstein’s own formulation in 5.61 concerns the limits of logic and of what can be said from within them.
Bertrand Russell
Russell supplies two problems that matter here: how to avoid contradiction in logical notation, and how a sentence’s grammar can conceal its logical structure.
Russell’s paradox and the vicious circle principle
Suppose every condition defines a set. Then we can form
R = \{x \mid x \notin x\}.
Substituting R for x gives
R \in R \iff R \notin R.
Either answer to the membership question entails its denial. The problem is the unrestricted assumption that allowed this set to be formed. Russell presents it among the contradictions motivating his 1908 theory of types, §I.
His vicious circle principle restricts definitions that presuppose a totality to which the defined item would itself belong. A hierarchy of types prevents the membership question above from being formed indiscriminately. This is a restriction on the formal language, with consequences for which mathematical definitions it permits. Russell 1908, §§II, IV-V.
type theory
Russell’s ramified theory of 1908 distinguishes orders of propositions and propositional functions according to the variables over which they quantify. Quantifying over individuals and quantifying over functions of individuals occupy different levels. A single undifferentiated domain of “all functions” would undo the restriction. Russell 1908, §V.

type theory
Russell’s ramified theory of 1908 distinguishes orders of propositions and propositional functions according to the variables over which they quantify. Quantifying over individuals and quantifying over functions of individuals occupy different levels. A single undifferentiated domain of “all functions” would undo the restriction. Russell 1908, §V.
The axiom of reducibility supplies a predicative function with the same truth-values, for every argument, as a given function of higher order. Here “predicative” means of the next order above its argument, so a predicative function of an individual is first-order. Russell uses the axiom to recover mathematical results that would otherwise require unrestricted quantification over functions. It adds an assumption; it leaves the distinction between the functions’ orders in place. Russell 1908, §VI, pp. 242-243.
theory of descriptions and logical fictions
In “On Denoting” (1905), Russell analyses a sentence of the form “the F is G” through existence, uniqueness, and predication. In modern notation:
\exists x\bigl(F(x) \land \forall y(F(y) \to y=x) \land G(x)\bigr).
There is exactly one thing satisfying F, and it satisfies G. If no such thing exists, the sentence is false under this analysis. A grammatical subject such as “the present king of France” therefore need not name an object for the whole sentence to receive an analysis. This is the useful lesson for reading the Tractatus: inspect how an expression functions in a proposition before deciding what entity it names.
early-Wittgenstein
pictures and logical form
A picture represents a possible arrangement of objects through the arrangement of its own elements. Its structure lets it present how things could stand; comparison with reality determines whether it is true. A false picture can still have sense. TLP 2.1-2.225.
An elementary proposition asserts that an atomic fact exists. Within the Tractatus, names stand for objects and their combination presents a possible state of affairs. This concerns propositions under logical analysis. It does not identify ordinary words with physical atoms or supply a model of vectors in an embedding space. TLP 3.203, 4.21-4.22.

Wittgenstein distinguishes what a proposition says from the logical form it displays. A proposition represents a possible situation, while the form that makes representation possible shows itself in that representation. This is the saying/showing distinction in 4.12-4.1212. The idea also explains his complaint at 3.331: Russell invokes what signs mean while laying down their syntactic rules. TLP 3.33-3.331, 4.12-4.1212.
criticism of Russell’s type theory
At 3.333, Wittgenstein examines the apparent self-application F(F(fx)). The repeated letter disguises two roles: the inner function takes the expression fx as its argument; the outer takes a function of that expression. In notation displaying those roles, the two occurrences would have different symbols. His proposed dissolution of Russell’s paradox depends on making the logical syntax clear. TLP 3.333.
This is an argument within his account of symbolism. It supplies no general prohibition on a program reading its own source, a recursive procedure, or a model generating a sentence about itself.
logic, ethics, and the ladder
Tautologies hold for every assignment of truth-values. Because they rule out no possible situation, they convey no factual information. Wittgenstein calls them sinnlos, lacking sense, and explicitly distinguishes them from unsinnig, nonsensical expressions. They still belong to logical symbolism. TLP 4.46-4.4611, 6.1-6.11.
His remarks on ethics and aesthetics concern the limits of factual description. At 6.41-6.421, value cannot be another contingent fact within the world. At 6.522, he says there is something inexpressible that shows itself. TLP 6.41-6.421, 6.522.

Then 6.54 turns the problem onto the book. The reader is asked to recognise its elucidations as nonsensical and discard the ladder after using it. How the book’s own sentences can guide a reader while failing its account of sense remains a problem for interpretation. TLP 6.54-7.

language games
The opening builders’ example in PI ties a call for a slab to an activity. Later examples include asking, joking, praying, and reporting. In §43, meaning as use is qualified: it applies to a large class of cases. It is a way into examining particular words, with their uses left available for inspection. PI §§2, 7, 23, 43.
The family-resemblance discussion likewise asks us to look at different games. Overlapping similarities can sustain a concept without one feature common to every example. It gives no reason to prohibit precise definitions where we have a use for them. PI §§65-71.
rules and private signs
Knowing a rule includes knowing how to continue. §§198-202 examine why another interpretation cannot settle every application: the interpretation would itself need applying. The distinction between following a rule and thinking one is following it belongs to a practice of use and correction. See forms of life. PI §§198-202.
The private-language discussion presses a related difficulty. If a sign refers to a sensation only its speaker could identify, and whatever seems right to that speaker counts as right, what distinguishes correct reuse from error? The diary in §258 makes that problem concrete. Ordinary descriptions of pain remain available; the proposed private standard is what needs explaining. PI §§243-258.

The philosophical task is to locate the confusion in a particular use of words. §§109-116 describe examining language and bringing words back to their ordinary applications; §133 speaks of multiple methods, including therapies. For a language model, a learned representation and participation in a practice are separate questions. The Tractatus asks how a proposition pictures a possible state of affairs; PI directs attention to use, correction, and continuation in an activity.

XLA (Accelerated Linear Algebra) compiles tensor computations for CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs. In JAX, jit stages a region of a program for compilation. This gives XLA several operations to optimize together: it can combine kernels, choose memory layouts, and reuse storage once values are dead. The executable still has to move data and perform the arithmetic. Architecture.
architecture
compilation pipeline
For a JAX function, the stages are:

Trace. JAX runs Python with tracers that describe input properties, usually shapes and dtypes, and records a jaxpr.
Lower. JAX converts that computation into StableHLO.
Compile. XLA optimizes the computation and generates an executable for the selected backend.
Execute. The runtime supplies device buffers and launches the executable.

These stages can be inspected separately. Lowered StableHLO shows what was passed to the compiler; optimized executable text shows later decisions. Neither is a timing measurement. JAX AOT API.
HLO: high-level operations
HLO represents tensor operations such as element-wise arithmetic, reductions, matrix products, and control flow. A logical tensor value does not prescribe a fresh physical allocation. Buffer assignment can reuse storage when lifetimes permit it. HLO operation semantics.
StableHLO
StableHLO is the versioned operation set at the framework/compiler boundary. It uses MLIR and specifies operations, types, and execution semantics. Its portability contract concerns the represented computation; runtime support and backend capabilities still determine where an exported program can run. Specification.
fusion
Consider this reduction over equal-length vectors:
s = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i+y_i z_i).
A separate element-wise multiply and add could each write a temporary vector. A fused implementation can compute intermediate values inside a kernel, avoiding those full-vector writes and reads. On a GPU this can also reduce launch overhead. XLA’s GPU backend uses fusion, generated kernels, and library calls. The backend and input shape determine which implementation it selects. GPU architecture.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
 
 
def compute(x, y, z):
  return jnp.sum(x + y * z)
 
 
x = jnp.arange(8, dtype=jnp.float32)
y = jnp.ones_like(x)
z = jnp.full_like(x, 2)
 
lowered = jax.jit(compute).lower(x, y, z)
print(lowered.as_text())
compiled = lowered.compile()
print(compiled.as_text())
print(compiled(x, y, z).block_until_ready())  # 44.0
The example exposes the compiler output for this machine. Counting source operators does not establish a kernel count. A reduction may need multiple stages, and fusion can increase register pressure or duplicate computation. Inspect the optimized program and a device trace before claiming that fusion helped.
core optimization passes
The useful questions concern where bytes and values go:

Algebraic simplification: which operations can disappear? Floating-point rewrites can change rounding, so compare numerical results at the precision the application needs. JAX numerical FAQ.
Layout assignment: how are logical dimensions stored? A transpose can sometimes become a layout choice; incompatible consumers can require a physical copy.
Buffer assignment: which dead values leave storage that another result can reuse?
Rematerialization: would recomputing a value reduce peak live memory enough to justify the extra work?

These are coupled decisions: eliminating an intermediate changes its lifetime, and changing a layout affects the kernels that can consume it. Compiler architecture, GPU layout and scheduling.
JAX integration
tracing mechanism
Python side effects occur while tracing. Ordinary print and mutation of a Python list do not become repeated device operations. Keep transformed functions pure and return state explicitly. JAX provides separate callback and debugging APIs when an effect is required. JIT tracing.
staged compilation
A compiled specialization depends on input properties and compilation settings. Changing shapes, dtypes, or static arguments can require another compilation. Define the jitted function outside a hot loop so its cache can be reused. A cache hit still executes the computation; cached compilation does not mean cached outputs. JIT caching.
control flow primitives
A Python if needs a concrete boolean during tracing. An input-dependent scalar predicate therefore needs a staged control-flow operation such as lax.cond. Both branches are traced and must return compatible structures, shapes, and dtypes. Control flow.

@jax.jit
def piecewise(x):
  return jax.lax.cond(x < 3, lambda t: 3.0 * t**2, lambda t: -4.0 * t, x)
 
 
print(piecewise(jnp.float32(2)))  # 12.0
print(piecewise(jnp.float32(4)))  # -16.0
A Python loop with a fixed trip count can be unrolled during tracing, enlarging the compiled graph. lax.scan represents a fixed-length loop with a carry whose shape and dtype stay fixed. That can reduce compilation size. Its runtime advantage depends on the workload; an unrolled linear scan still performs linear work.
dynamic shapes
JAX export supports symbolic dimensions so one exported program can cover a family of shapes. This saves repeated tracing and lowering. The exported program can still compile separately for each concrete shape. Shape-polymorphic export therefore gives no general promise of one machine executable for every size. Shape polymorphism.
autodiff through XLA
JAX applies automatic-differentiation transformations before the resulting computation is compiled. For example, jax.jit(jax.grad(loss)) stages the gradient computation. Choosing forward or reverse mode belongs to the JAX transformation being requested. XLA then optimizes the resulting program.
jax.checkpoint controls which autodiff residuals are saved and which are recomputed during the backward pass. The memory and arithmetic tradeoff depends on the checkpoint boundary and the function. Gradient checkpointing.
backend code generation
The backend chooses target-specific implementations, including generated code and optimized library calls. CPU, GPU, and TPU executables have different schedules and memory constraints. A source expression alone cannot tell us which kernel, library, or communication algorithm ran.
PJRT exposes device discovery, buffers, compilation, and executable invocation through a common API. It is a runtime interface; supporting PJRT does not mean that a plugin must use XLA internally. PJRT overview.
performance characteristics
compilation overhead
Suppose compilation takes time C, a warmed compiled call takes t_c, and a reference call takes t_r. Ignoring other startup costs and assuming these times stay fixed, compilation pays for itself after N calls when
C + Nt_c < Nt_r.
